The House resumed from Monday, April 6 consideration of Biil C-3, to amend the Criminal Code as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, and Motion No. 2 (Mr. Woolliams).

Mr. Speaker, the United Nations declaration on the elimination of all forms of racial discrimination which was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on November 21, 1963, was supported by Canada. It provides as follows:
The necessity of speedily eliminating racial discrimination throughout the world, in all its forms and manifestations, and of securing understanding of and respect for the dignity of the human person.
I submit that is an important part of Canadian foreign policy. Surely, the provisions before the House in Bill C-3 are consistent with that policy and inconsistent with any other conclusion than that we are genuinely acting against unjust discrimination.
An editorial in the Toronto Globe and Mail this morning, Mr. Speaker, expressed the view that Bill C-3 is a clear attempt to legislate morality and that its main section would make it a crime to communicate statements that promote hatred. The editorial goes on to ask why. Then, it continues:
Not because anything follows from that, not because public order is disturbed, not because windows are broken or a mob becomes unruly, not because anyone is endangered or because there is a breach of the peace or even the likelihood of a breach of the peace, it simply says it is wrong to promote hate, period.
Hate Propaganda
I respectfully disagree with the tone of the editorial. It completely overlooks the evil effects on the lives and social attitudes of classes singled out for hatred, which in some cases leaves scars and wounds on their minds and personalities, but also overlooks the tendency to single out groups for social discrimination of a deplorable nature. Also, Mr. Speaker, this same editorial overlooks the fact that the bill is not designed to prevent hatred, period. But rather the bill is designed to prohibit hatred directed against any identifiable group which is specifically defined in proposed new section 267A(4) as, "any section of the public distinguished by colour, race, religion, or ethnic origin." Thus, here we have a classic example of a nationally read newspaper giving a wrong impression of the provisions of a proposed criminal statutory amendment.
The subject matter of Bill C-3 has been considered by a royal commission. The bill has been thoroughly discussed in committee, and now is the time to support it in this House. It represents a major landmark in the extension of the laws of libel and slander to cover vulnerable groups in our society and to protect those identifiable groups from the vile abuse of verbal pollution expressed in the form of hatred.
Why? Because minorities need protection, and the Canadian standard of fair play for all demands it. That is why, Mr. Speaker. We can all recall the events which occurred prior to and during the Second World War when, by use of expressions of hatred, hatred led to genocide, and millions of innocent people of the Jewish faith were slaughtered in Europe.
I suggest that hatred breeds contempt, and that the result in society is a form of social class distinction which is abhorrent to all Canadians. The scars created by expressions of hatred based on discrimination against colour, race or creed, in many cases last forever. The soul and the spirit of Canadians require a standard of conduct which will eliminate the stigma of second class citizenship.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, the bill has profound educational value as a measure to enhance the strength and spirit of true Canadian respect for the dignity of man. To me, we are strengthening the bonds of citizenship in Canadian society by demonstrating the intention and determination of the Canadian people to prevent social class distinction, and to place those in identifiable groups on exactly the same level of respect

April 7. 1970
Hate Propaganda
and regard as all other Canadians. This bill will be a victory for the dignity of the rights of Canadians. As a lawyer, I see this bill as a specific example of the rule of law whereby "all are equal in the eyes of the law", and perhaps this bill expresses the view that all are socially equal and not despised or discriminated against by reason of race, religion, colour or ethnic origin in the eyes of the law as well as in the soul of man.
In these days of television, radio and fast communication it is sound legislative planning to provide such humane criminal legislation. Thus, we in this place will in some measure remove the psychological pain and the unfortunate doubts and uncertainties which in some cases pervade the minds of individuals in minority groups, to their lasting misery and resentment. We shall prohibit hatred in the forms expressed in the bill by criminal laws of restraint, and thus remove from identifiable groups the stigma left by the expression of that hatred.
We in Parliament do not seek to pry into the minds of men, but we do intend to prohibit acts of discrimination against identifiable groups. Mr. Speaker, when I think of all those Canadians who sacrificed their lives in war, in the war against tyranny and racial discrimination, I do believe that in a very real and lasting sense we here today are supporting the cause for which they valiantly fought and died.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me first pay tribute to those who have already discussed this matter in the House. I think this is one of the occasions when hon. members rise to great heights in their attention, discussion, and contributions to the subject matter which is before this House for its decision. I say this advisedly because unfortunately we have heard a few really snide comments upon the nature and the quality of the discussions in this House. That may be all very well for those few people who think this is a place which should be an abattoir, swimming in blood at all times, rather than a place providing grave and solemn opportunity for the discussion of serious issues. This has been one of those occasions, and I pay tribute to hon. members who have made their speeches along those lines, although I may not and probably will not agree with everything that has been said.
Now, Mr. Speaker, because this sort of debate touches the consciences, the feelings, the emotions, and the background-possibly to some extent there is an hereditary aspect

to it-people will take different positions. We saw evidence of this yesterday with some members on the government side. I mention in particular the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hogarth), who proposed a motion with which I was in sympathy. If he had been able to persuade five of his colleagues to stand and the matter had been put to a vote I would have voted for it. But he was not supported by a large number of his colleagues and so the matter did not come to a vote. However, I pause to say it is quite obvious that a great many members opposite must now be discussing in their seats what took place yesterday.
I have no doubt that as time passes, and as this debate progresses, there will be members on this side of the House who may differ from the things I have to say, who may differ from the majority of the people in their party, and that may be this party or it may be the New Democratic Party. I would think it passing strange, Mr. Speaker, and I say this through you to hon. members of this House, if there were not to some extent some parting of the ways in the approaches which many hon. members take to this particular measure because of the issues which are involved.
I agree with what the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) said yesterday when he pointed out that no particular, sudden emergency has arisen which calls into being the need for this legislation. No particular public situation has come about. There is no clear and present danger. As a matter of fact, there has been a presistent, stubborn and very well organized campaign to bring these new laws into effect, and it will ultimately succeed.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
I do not fault the people who have pursued this campaign. It is their democratic right. It is proper for them to do so. I do not fault them for that, and I do not say the government should not have introduced the bill because of that. I simply pause to say that in 1964 there was a private members' public bill introduced by I think it was at that time the hon. member for Cartier. I spoke on that. The bill was not quite the same, but it dealt primarily with the issues which are before the House today. I opposed part of it then, as I oppose part of it today. Some of the things I said then I am going to repeat today and I am fortified in this because after six years of consideration, contemplation and discussion of this issue, I hold the same views even more strongly than I did then.
April 7. 1970

As has been indicated, Mr. Speaker, there are three aspects of this bill and then there are some consequential matters which follow.
I have no d.ffieulty in accepting the proposals contained in section 267A dealing with genocide and I doubt very much if there will ever be any prosecutions launched in this country. However, the passage of this particular section constitutes an adherance to an international obligation which this country accepted some time ago. I have no hesitation in saying that if this section stood by itself I would have no problems at all.
I differ to some extent from my colleague the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) in that I would not be too afraid of accepting the first part of section 267B, the proposed new section of the Criminal Code, which provides:
Every one who, by communicating statements in any public place, incites hatred against any identifiable group where such incitement is likely to lead to a breach of the peace-
I am reinforced in my view that this would not be too difficult a proposition to accept because it does contain a safeguard. Hon. members who have practised law, and all hon. members who have had occasion to deal with the Criminal Code, will realize that there is in fact this safeguard, that in order for there to be a conviction it must be established that the incitement is likely to lead to a breach of the peace.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I abhor violence-we all abhor violence. We have seen too much of it. I am afraid that in too many deliberative assemblies in the world today there is not that opportunity to reflect the views, the thinking, wishes and desires of the people. We have too much domination by an executive and not enough opportunity by the elected branch to pursue their task for the people. One of the reasons we have this violence, and why it will continue, has been the failure of the deliberative bodies to exercise the right which they must exercise to give the views, thoughts, wishes and aspirations of the people full consideration.
Because of that, Mr. Speaker, when I see this particular subsection which says that where there is likely to be a breach of the peace an offence would be brought about, I am prepared to accept it. To that extent, I am prepared to confirm what I said earlier, that there are differences, there are distinctions between the thinking and the views of hon. members of this House and even between hon. members of the same party. To that

extent, I would part company from my distinguished colleague, the learned and hon. member for Calgary North.
I would point out, however, that I am not as much concerned about it as I otherwise would be, Mr. Speaker. To substantiate that point, I refer to the speech I made on July 10, 1964 when, in dealing with this very same issue 1 said, as recorded on page 5359 of Hansard:
The hon. member quite properly pointed his finger at the word "person"-
We were dealing with the question of defamatory libel then.
-and said that the word "person" having been used in the Criminal Code, this automatically excludes actions which are directed against a class.
This was to distinguish whether or not an action would lie under the Criminal Code for inciting hatred of a class of people as distinguished from an individual.
At first blush I think that is a very sound argument, but I would refer the hon. member, who is from the province of Quebec, to a Quebec case. I do not have the case itself here, but it is referred to in The Canadian Abridgement, volume 13, and in column 436 I read these words:
... a charge of publishing a defamatory libel against the Roman Catholic clergy of a particular diocese does not disclose an offence. Section 317... specifically refers to a "person" and the definition of "person" in section 2(13) is not sufficiently wide to include an unincorporated group-
The citation then goes on:
An indictment will lie at the common law, and the common law is in effect in this country to the extent to which it has not been-
-taken away.
-the indictment in such case must allege (and the crown must prove) that the tendency of the libel was to excite hatred against all members of the class and to provoke a breach of the peace.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, by the common law which still exists in this country, it would be possible to lay a charge under almost the same facts and circumstances as set out in the first part of this proposed new section 267B (1).
For that reason, I am not too concerned with the argument of the hon. member for Calgary North, and I disagree on this aspect of his amendment. In the very rare and almost unprecedented circumstances which could bring about the laying of a charge under this subsection if passed, as it will be passed no doubt, it would be the same as an information laid under common law so we are not losing anything and we get this protection. Hon. members must think about this.

April 7, 1970

In order for a conviction to be brought about, at some time or other a judge or a jury, and ultimately a court of appeal, will have to say that the statements made in this public place were of such a nature that they were liable to lead to violence, to a breach of the peace. Abhoring as I do the thought that violence could become a way of life, I would go along with the section because it has that protection. Thus I do not need to move, as I otherwise might have moved, an amendment to the motion we are now considering because we have the protection of the existing common law which covers this particular area.
Any reservations which I had about 267B <1), Mr. Speaker, have grown to such substantial doubts with regard to 267B (2), that I could not accept it under any circumstances. I agree with much of what was said yesterday about the inherent difficult and dangerous circumstances which would be brought about if 267B (2) were passed. It would lead the law enforcement agencies and the courts of this land into a very serious situation. It is bad law; it is bad philosophy and the facts are bad. It is not the kind of law which a country such as Canada should have. Much as I appreciate the views of other people, and much as I accept the views of many of my friends, I could not under any condition support a bill which contains a clause of this kind.
Life and society ought to consist of a continuous process of the circulation of creeds and philosophies, each in turn being conceived in the conflict of ideas and often born to the accompaniment of passion and anger. Each rises, blooms, and then fades, but contributes much to the values and the philosophies which succeed. On this account alone, we have a grave responsibility not to diminish the opportunity, not only to permit but to strongly encourage the clash between people and ideas. When we stop doing this, sir, I say to you, and through you to my colleagues, that the motor which powers society will run out of fuel and our civilization will be on its way to perishing.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
We wonder at times what will be the interpretation of some of the clauses of this bill. What will be the problems to which these clauses will give rise. What is to be the interpretation of hatred? It is all very well for my friends to say, "Look at the dictionary", but the dictionary is not good enough; it gives no answer on an issue like this. What I may consider to be hatred may be something quite different in the mind of the person to whom I

am addressing my remarks. How is there to be an opportunity for the conflict of ideas and the clash of opinions if we are to be inhibited in the fullest expression of our views? Hatred to me, my friends, my family and the people I associate with may mean one thing; it may mean something entirely different to other people. What will it mean to a judge? In the final analysis, in any jurisprudence on this issue, the court will probably say that it is what reasonable people conceive, under certain reasonable conditions, to constitute hatred. That will mean that hatred will be what the majority of the people of the country consider hatred to be. The majority will be imposing their interpretation of hatred on the minority. I do not accept that for a minute, especially since this may mean that matters arising out of the communication of ideas which are not likely to lead to violence will be the basis of convictions. I cannot accept that in any circumstances.
I raise another thought. How are we to consider existing material? What about existing books? What about films and what about scripts? There are books published 100 years ago which, in my opinion, contain phrases, sentences and whole paragraphs that under this law, if passed, would constitute breaches of the criminal law. If I were to give to my hon. and distinguished friend, the leader of my party, (Mr. Stanfield) a book which contained this material I could be convicted of "communicating" within the meaning of this particular clause.

Members of the government and members of the committee, he said, who had studied this bill had tried to achieve a reasonable balance, a reasonable reconciliation, so that the conflicting legitimate interests of freedom of expression, on the one hand, and the protection of reputation and group identity, on the other, are balanced. "Feelings of the community", "abhorrence"; "what is believed to be reasonable by the government"-that is exactly the kind of rationale and justification for the limitation of free speech which liberals have fought for centuries. It is extraordinary what societies will consider at any time to be abhorrent. It was because the Athenians thought the views of Socrates were abhorrent that he was put to death. It was because the Romans felt the views of Christ were abhorrent that he was crucified. It is because Protestants have felt the views of Catholics to be abhorrent that they have tried to exerminate them-and Catholics the views of Protestants. Moslems have believed the views of Christians to be so abhorrent that they would prevent them from being disseminated. The church believed the views of Galileo to be abhorrent and tried to extirpate them from the books by command.
In this century, the people of Tennessee have thought that views on evolution were so abhorrent that they should not be allowed to be propagated. Within the last 15 years people in the Uniled States have believed that views of Communism were so un-American and so abhorrent that they should not be allowed to be advocated.
Liberals have fought for centuries, as I have said, to develop bases for the defence of free speech on a basis other than the generalized conscience and moral feeling of the community. They go back to Pericles, 25 centuries ago, who said that in Athens we allow all

men to come, and all men to speak and say what they will, and let all men judge because
we have confidence in the discrimination and judgment of the people in our society.
This is the kind of view which John Stuart Mill expressed in the last century when he suggested we must allow ideas which are abhorrent and wicked to us to be presented and discussed because only in free discussion will one find the truth; only in the clash of ideas will one be able to determine what the truth is. By saying to a man that you will not allow him to present his views because they are so wicked or abhorrent, you are denying the possibilities of persuading him through argument. You are also denying yourself the chance of re-affirming and strengthening the views that you have by presenting them in contested arguments.
Liberals have drawn a distinction between actions and thoughts. They have said actions should be limited when they harm the interests of the community. They have said that thought should only be limited-this is indeed the whole theme and spirit that infuses John Stuart Mill's essays, "On Liberty"-when it transgresses specific and identifiable individual interests.
That is the principle which liberals have followed through the ages; the principle not that an expression was abhorrent, not that it was offensive, not that it was in bad taste, not that it went against standards of decency, but that it transgressed specific, identifiable, concrete, individual interests, not a vague, outlawing expression of opinion in one category, but a transgression of specific individual interests. Even in those circumstances, as Mill suggested, liberals have held that the advantage to society of having free expression of views greatly outweighs the rather minimal interference with an individual's interest which could occur with the expression of free thought.
The whole liberal belief has been that the wellspring of social progress lies in allowing people to express all their views, bizarre, wicked and pernicious though they may be, because they have believed that "truth is not put to flight in a free encounter," and that it is on this truth that social progress is dependent. Once we start to say that we can outlaw one set of ideas and prevent their expression because we consider them to be so abhorrent to us, or a sizable group in our community, it is very easy to go on and to find other views which are also abhorrent and to consider that these, too, shall be ruled out of discussion and

out of free expression. Indeed, that has happened, as I have just said, many, many times throughout history.
The liberal principle has been that you do not create sacred cows beyond the realm of discussion and contestation, and that when you create sacred cows you are weakening the foundations of liberal democratic society. Liberals have believed our society is strong enough, calm enough and tolerant enough that dark thoughts should be brought out and dealt with in the light of day through debate and discussion. A democracy which has lost faith in the judgment of its citizens has lost faith in itself. That is essentially what this legislation says to us. It says we do not have sufficient confidence in the judgment of our citizens that they will look upon these pernicious ideas for what they are and assess them correctly. We have so little faith in their judgment that we will prevent these pernicious ideas from being expressed at all.
I have not lost faith in the judgment of our citizens. I do not find in this proposed legislation a practical approach to dealing with what prejudices there are in our society. Moreover, it confounds and attacks a basic principle of what I believe liberal society should be. I cannot as a liberal, in conscience, support this legislation and shall, therefore, vote against it.

The amendment is commended in the name of freedom of speech, freedom of assembly and freedom of the press. I believe we would be doing a disservice to a sound concept of what is involved in freedom of speech if we turn down, by a false cry of freedom of speech, a reasonable limitation upon that freedom of speech imposed in the public interest by this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, about six years ago I had the privilege of standing in this House and supporting a colleague who is no longer here, Mr. Milton Klein, the then member for Cartier. I supported and seconded his motion in respect of a private member's bill dealing with the type of situation which is now covered by a government bill. I felt it would be important to remember what my colleague, Mr. Klein, did during the private members' hour in the form of a private member's bill to bring what I call a great social problem to the attention of Parliament and this country.
I do not suppose there is any piece of legislation on any issue that has received greater thought over a longer period of time. As has been stated in this debate, the principle involved in the original private member's bill received consideration at various stages. It was discussed in committee. It was before the Senate twice and was before the former committee on external affairs. My friend, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), played a very active part in the proceedings before that committee. I am sure he will remind me if I am not correct when I say that I believe there were very lengthy hearings at which briefs pro and con were received from many people, and at which time people who did not have closed minds appeared as witnesses. These witnesses were people who understood the great social implication of what we were endeavouring to do. The government of the day decided that this question was important enough for the government itself to accept the responsibility of placing this legislation before us.
I wish to congratulate this government, and particularly the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), for taking the responsibility of bringing this matter before us for our consideration. I do not think I have listened to any
April 7. 1970

debate in which there has been less acrimony and less personal vindictiveness, such as we sometimes see in this House. I have been very pleased with the debate. I certainly accept the sincerity of all the opinions expressed. However, as a Liberal-and 1 address this particular statement to my friend across the way in the same party who feels he cannot support the bill-I fully support this bill. I have been fighting for such a measure for the past six years, as have a number of other people. Up until now many of the contributions have been made by members of this House who, by profession, practice law. I have had the feeling we are getting bogged down in the legal technicalities of the bill. Once this legislation is passed, if the House sees fit to pass it, the matter of the legal application of it may end up in the courts, where I suggest the points of law should be argued rather than in the House of Commons.
Along this same line, may I say that the other day I read some comments by the economist Galbraith about the way to battle inflation. He suggested one of the difficulties in respect of what we are doing now is that the experts, the professors and economists, are the only people who are having their say. So, today I stand here not as a professional person but possibly as a representative of the man on the street. I believe it might be helpful to hear from the man on the street in respect of this legislation.
In 1966, the Toronto Daily Star sent out reporters on the street to interview ordinary Canadian citizens about this matter. I would like to place the result of this interview on the record. No matter what type of a law we pass in the House of Commons, or what type of law is recommended by the law officers, I have a feeling a law is good only if it is accepted by the public. There are many laws on the books these days that are observed in the breach much more than by compliance. It makes a ridiculous situation when we have laws that are not observed, possibly because public opinion and the ordinary good, common horse sense of the man in the street have not been taken into account when the laws have been drafted.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
In this particular interview, the question was asked:
Should free speech be allowed in public parks-?
I want to put these answers on the record because there are a lot of hon. members who have made contributions who have been

wondering about the cut-off point at which free speech is no longer free speech because the purpose of it is to destroy the freedom of other people. Here is a lady, Mrs. Sadie Denley, a housewife, who says:
I believe in freedom of speech-as one's right under democracy. But the line has to be drawn somewhere when inflammatory speeches tend to incite the crowd to riot and violence, resulting in harm to someone. It is only sensible to exercise some restraint over speeches.
Here is Harry Jackson, a salesman, who says:
One's first reaction to any kind of censorship, particularly in speech, is to think of a police state. One should be free to voice opinions in what one believes. But to carry this to the point of accusing a certain person or race, colour and creed, or condemning them, goes beyond freedom of speech. This is downright unacceptable to any intelligent person.
Here is Norman Thornley, a salesman, who says:
When a speech tends to insult one's religion, race or colour, whether of an individual or collectively, in a public park or anywhere, then it constitutes slander. Preventing this kind of speech isn't censorship. It's just a sensible, legal restraint.
Here is Bill Graham, a sales representative, who says:
As with any privilege, it can be abused.
He is speaking of freedom of speech.
No one has a right to a freedom that would permit excessiveness that results in violence, destruction and harm. This constitutes an attack on society. And preventing this extreme does not constitute censorship.
Here is Harold Nissenthall, a company employee, who says:
Every individual should be allowed to voice his feelings and opinions. But singling out some individual or group, and hurling abuse and insults at them, can never be regarded as coming within the legal claim of freedom of speech.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker and colleagues, that the opinion of the ordinary man in the street, the man who does not perhaps understand the technicalities of law but does understand some of the social problems and social evils we have in our society, is equally valid and may be more important than some of the technical legal arguments that we have heard in this House of Commons today.
Not because it was a particularly good speech but because it went to the centre of my thinking, away back in 1964 as a matter of fact, I would like to quote from a speech which I made in the House of Commons at that time. I would like to say that, in my judgment, these people who are able to spread hatred because of the present lack in

the law have in their hands a time bomb, a poison vial, that can really be more destructive of our society and our human relations than possibly a military bomb.
On that occasion I said:
These enemies of society, these wreckers and destroyers of other people's lives-
Because that is what they are.
-use freedom of speech to destroy other freedoms equally important-
Perhaps freedom from fear should be considered to be a right of Canadians equal to freedom of speech, and also freedom from persecution. Hate propaganda racists are people who are so bitter in their hatred that they blame other people for their frustrations, and the next step most of them take is to use democracy to destroy democracy. They use freedom of speech for themselves to destroy the freedom from fear of other people.
The racists always use these methods. Surely the persecuted, the good citizens-
I am taking this out of the context of talking only about one group, a minority of people in this country. Canada, Mr. Speaker, is a country of minorities.
Surely the persecuted, the good citizens, deserve the same sympathy and consideration and freedom which apparently exists under the present laws for the rotten racists and their followers.
Surely, the good people have a right to the protection of some law that the absence of law now gives to the racists.
These.. .unbalanced bitter people are using our laws to make fools of us all.
We are in a new era in a troubled time, Mr. Speaker. We are in an era of great disturbance in societies all over the world, and I believe we have to achieve a new dimension in human relations if society is going to hold together. I cannot think of any country better equipped than Canada, that has so few of the problems bothering other societies in the world, to encourage the establishment of good human personal relations as an example to the rest of the world of what a liberal, open society should be doing.
Violence and the threat of violence endanger our society. They endanger the peace. We must counteract within the framework of the law the racists who are here. They are in our midst. They are here to disturb us. As I say, we must counteract within the framework of the law these racists, otherwise violence as a principle has won out over law as a guiding principle upon which a civilized society should be based. If we have no laws now to

protect the basic right of people to live undisturbed, unthreatened lives, then surely we must make those laws. As individuals we cannot take the law into our own hands, although I can imagine and I know of instances in this country and in other societies where people driven to frustration because they do not have the protection of the rest of society, reach the point where they say, "Nobody will protect us. There is no law to protect us; therefore we must take the law into our own hands." One does not have to look very far from the borders of our own country to see where this sort of thing is taking place. I would think that a very small step at this time, by way of a very mild law, may preclude the necessity in the future of something that would be abhorrent to us all. I refer to the passage of some law that would have authoritarian strength in it of a kind that we would not want.
We cannot take the law into our own hands or we would destroy the very thing we are trying to produce, a country and a world of peace and order, in which we may all live lives of creativeness and purpose without the fear of having our freedoms destroyed. And, Mr. Speaker, all I ask is the same protection, the very same protection for the good people in this country, for the non-racists in this country, for the decent majority of citizens in this country, as presently exists for the racists who are apparently determined to destroy our Canadian society. I will certainly be supporting this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment that is before the House. I do so for a number of reasons, some of them already aptly expressed by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Roberts). In passing, I must say it was interesting to note the differences in opinion between the hon. member for York-Simcoe and the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Walker).
It is all well and good to go out and interview people on the street about a proposed piece of legislation designed to limit the freedom of speech, and ask them whether they like it and whether at any time freedom of speech should be limited, but we cannot place much reliance on the opinions that are gathered that way when the persons interviewed have not had the intent of the bill explained to them. It really lends very little weight to the argument used by the member for York Centre (Mr. Walker).

[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I have nothing against the provisions in the bill which outlaw genocide, and I suppose nobody will find fault with that aspect of it, but the rest of the bill gives me a great deal of concern. We can talk about guarding freedom of speech, but we must of course accept the responsibility that goes along with all our freedom. If in this piece of legislation we must place some limits on the freedom of speech, are we not really just getting out of accepting responsibility for doing so? I think we are. We are shelving our responsibility by saying that the society in which we live will no longer accept responsibility for its acts and, therefore, we have to legislate control. Surely, in this country we have not gone that far, though some people may believe that society is slipping. This piece of legislation might be justifiable in some of the underdeveloped countries where there is a tendency to create ha'red, riot and violence and so on, but as one of the better educated countries of the world surely we have not slipped that far. Surely, with our level of education, we are above that.
The bill attempts to define hate literature in this way:
"hate propaganda" means any writing, sign or visible representation that advocates or promotes genocide or the communication of which by any person would constitute an offence under section 267B;
Now, section 267B is the one that worries me, Mr. Speaker. It reads:
Every one who, by communicating statements in any public place, incites hatred against any identifiable group-
I ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) or any other member of this House, through you, Mr. Speaker, what would have happened if a bill like this had been in the hands of some of the governors in the southern United States who were faced with people trying to bring about better conditions? Would these people not have been accused of inciting riots, inciting acts of violence and hatred? Would the governors not have used legislation like this to confine and regulate the minority? I do not want to name any of these governors but we have seen them on television and have had them here in our country. We have seen their attitude to some of the justifiable uprisings that have taken place, and here I am going back to the beginning of the recent upheavals in the United States six or seven years ago. What would a bill like this have done, and how would it have been used?

Many members have said that this bill will never be used. If the person who may use it is fair and broadminded, then no harm will come from it. In trying to protect minorities, we may well be harming or limiting the expression of thought of those minorities. I cannot emphasize this point too much. When we think of the uprising in the country to the south of us, and I am thinking of some of the southern states where there has been an uprising of an identifiable group for a justifiable purpose, a bill like this could have been used to control the measures taken to bring about social change and better conditions.
One of the good things that may come out of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is that it may limit the CBC, something which nobody has been able to do. Nobody has been able to limit what we see on our television screens. Some years ago the leader of the Nazi movement in the United States, as I think it was called, a Mr. Rockwell, was brought to Canada. Had this bill been passed then, I suppose he could have been accused of promoting hatred in a public place. I am sure the television screen could be defined as such. One could say the same of Stokely Carmichael and some of the other agitators on the North American continent who are brought to this country from time to time by the CBC. So perhaps, Mr. Speaker, one good thing that will come out of this bill is that somebody somewhere will place some control on the CBC. That is a very negligible amount of good to come out of a piece of legislation which could otherwise be so very harmful, which could disrupt and divide a relatively united country. People who have worked side by side and fought for social change are divided on this legislation. Some say it is not necessary and some say it will never be used. Why bring it in if it is so poor?
What are the benefits of this legislation and how is the application of it going to affect the man on the street? Well, he is going to be limited. The committee changes subsection 2 of section 267B and added "other than in private conversation". I suppose this means that one has to be talking to more than one person, but it still does not mean that one can say what one wants to two or three people in one's own home. The effect, therefore, is limiting to that extent and changes the whole principle of our legal system. This afternoon Your Honour suggested that it creates equality in the eyes of the law; I think Your Honour saw a lot more in the bill than I do. I think it changes the whole concept of our law

that a man is innocent until proven guilty. If a man is accused under this law he is automatically guilty and then has to use the defences provided in the measure to justify his statements or publications. If in using these defences he can prove that the statements were absolutely true, he is not guilty but it is up to him to prove it.
Section 267B (3) reads:
(b)	if, in good faith, he expressed or attempted to establish by argument an opinion upon a religious subject;
This means he could use the defence that he was only expressing the idea to promote discussion and argument, that he did not believe what he said. I suppose he could get around the charge that way. I believe that defence would make it very difficult to convict anybody who had good legal advice.
Section 267B (3) (c) reads:
(c)	if the statements were relevant to any subject of public interest, the discussion of which was for the public benefit, and if on reasonable grounds he believed them to be true;
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I suppose one could incite a riot if one thought it was for the public good. I watched television once and saw a member of the Ontario Legislature, Stephen Lewis, interviewed. He as much as said, "Riots are all right; a little violence does not hurt. Sometimes it brings about change, and that is good for the country." He more or less said that on television. Clearly, he was indicating that violence was in the public interest; that it was good for the public. This is a matter that is dealt with in subparagraph (c). I ask, were the people who attempted to burn the Murray Hill garage acting in the public interest? True, they were not an identifiable group, but violence and hatred were certainly displayed in their actions. One man was killed.
To me, this is poor legislation. What is the aim of the Minister of Justice? In which direction is he leading Canadian law and our legal system? I am no lawyer, but having looked at the defences set out in the bill I can safely say that it is a good thing the Minister of Justice is not in practice and attempting to defend someone who has contravened the provisions of this bill. I do not think a practising lawyer would have introduced a bill like this with so many weaknesses and loopholes.
Subparagraph (c) reads in part:
-and if on reasonable grounds he believed them to be true;-

If charged, I suppose I would have to convince the judge and jury that I really believed my utterances were true. I would then say, "I am sorry Your Honour; I thought my utterances were true, but I now realize they were not true. Please do not convict me." I suppose a lenient judge might say, "I believe you had reasonable grounds for believing your utterances to be true and, as a result of your defence, the court cannot convict you." I should get off scot-free. Will this bill not benefit the so-called martyr, the real kook who advocates violence and who puts out hate literature that is directed against an identifiable group? Will passage of this bill not mean that the would-be martyr will gain a platform for the dissemination of his ideas? There will be court cases which will be reported by newspapers, and the would-be martyr's utterances and hatreds will be fully reported. That is the type of person this bill will benefit, the person who wishes to become a martyr, who wishes to be tried in order to secure that publicity which will further his views in our society.
An example being the Chicago Seven.

Yes, the Chicago Seven. Subparagraph (d) reads in part:
-if, in good faith, he intended to point out, for the purpose of removal, matters producing or tending to produce feelings of hatred towards an identifiable group in Canada.
What that means it is hard to say. The bill is weak because the defences enumerated would allow 'almost anybody to escape the punishment he may or may not deserve. As I say, passage of this bill will mean that would-be martyrs will be assured of newspaper coverage of their trials. They hope thus to publish their views. Really, no man will be convicted under this bill unless he, himself, wishes to be convicted. To my mind, the bill will limit the workings of the CEC, benefit the would-be martyr and do little else for the good of our society. Surely, we could better spend our time in this House promoting better education and better understanding instead of promoting existing divi:ions.
Hear, hear.

Because that is what the bill does; it promotes existing divisions. It says there is no cure for them and therefore we will penalize anyone who tries to create divisions. That is a very negative way of thinking, and a surprising way of thinking for the
April 7. 1970

Minister of Justice who I thought at one time was rather forward thinking.

I urge the Minister of Justice to withdraw the bill. It ought to be withdrawn; and the reprinted version should include the clause respecting genocide, but nothing else.
Mr. Speaker-

I see
the government has 'at least one supporter.

I should like to think that there are some supporters of this bill on the opposition side as well. With respect to the sum total of the arguments which have been made for the amendment and against the bill, I must say that, while some of the arguments have been cogent, many, I fear, have been specious. As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) said last night, they are sophistical arguments.
A few minutes ago the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) raised the question whether certain kinds of riots would be exempt from the provisions of the bill. The defences he referred to are not defences to offences under the public order section; they are defences to offences dealing with the distribution of hate propaganda, and there is no such question which really 'arises as a result of this particular bill.
I trust the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) will not object if I single out his address for particular attention. I believe it is fair to say he was the official spokesman for the opposition on this subject. In his speech yesterday he referred many times to the words "ridicule and contempt". Of course, the tradi'ional common law phrase with respect to criminal defamation was the phrase "hatred, ridicule and contempt". I am sure all hon. members know that the word "ridicule" was dropped by the Cohen Committee in its wording respecting the new offence of group defamation. The word "contempt" was eliminated by the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs during its deliberations. The only word that remains of this original common law triad is the word "hatred". Therefore, the references the hon. member for Calgary North made in his rhetoric to ridicule and contempt are, I submit, beside the point.

He also referred to the speeches of Kennedy and King. I am not sure which Kennedy he meant. In any case, I would suggest that he would be hard put to find statements by those men which are incitements to hatred. Men like Kennedy and King do not need to resort to hatred, do not need to resort to attacks on another person who is a member of the natural groups protected under this bill, in order to make their points adequately. Nor need anyone resort to such attacks in order to carry on the kind of dialogue which is necessary in a democratic society.

Will the hon. member permit a question? I did not say these men were either professing or promoting hatred. But would he not agree that it was because of hate-it may have been paranoic hate-that Robert Kennedy was assassinated?
I agree, and that is the very type of hate this bill is attempting to curb.
Hear, hear.

A substantive argument, although I am not sure that it is more substantial, is that with regard to selective protection for groups. Selective protection is not unknown in the law, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian Bill of Rights, which was originally sponsored by hon. members who now sit in opposition and which was heartily endorsed by hon. members on this side of the House, selects, among the rights it will protect, the freedom of speech, freedom of assembly and so on. It does not put on the same level the equality of the sexes, the right to privacy and the liberty of employment.
The question is not whether there is selective protection, but what is the basis of the selection. We should know that the protection is not, despite some of the comments which have been made, proposed to be given to groups. The protection is to be given to individuals in their capacity as members of a group; it is to be given to individuals who may be attacked because they are members of a group. The whole thrust of this legislation seeks to protect individuals in a way they were not protected at common law and in a way they were not protected by statute previously.
After all, Mr. Speaker, in earlier centuries we did not have the same consciousness of groups that we now have. We did not realize that what might be said about a man, his group capacity and his membership in one of

April 7, 1970
Hate Propaganda
these basic groups, could hurt him just as much as a comment that was made about him directly as an individual with reference to his own individualizing characteristics.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The selectivity of protection of this bill is its very strength. The basis of this selectivity is to protect a man in his membership in those groups which are most natural and most basic to him, the groups to which he belongs almost by reason of his very being. As the history of mankind shows, group membership has produced the greatest degree of hatred throughout human history. This is the basis of the protection and the selectivity of the protection which this legislation attempts to give. This selectivity is its strength.
Another argument made by the hon. member for Calgary North deals with the adequacy of the present Criminal Code. The hon. member referred to section 60 and the sections immediately following which deal with seditious libel. I submit that this argument and his reference to the Boucher case reveal a misunderstanding of the focus of this legislation with which we are now dealing in comparison to the traditional sanction against sedition.
Sedition is a concept which has to do with the relationship of the individual and the state directly. It classifies as undesirable conduct certain kinds of agitation by individuals which is directed against the government and attempts to overthrow the government or, in earlier days, the person of the monarch. This is not the purpose of this legislation. This legislation is not directed to protecting the government, but to protecting other people in society. It is directed to protecting some of the weaker and more vulnerable people against those who may attack them. It is not an attempt by the government to protect itself. The focus of this legislation is not the same as legislation dealing with sedition. The comments made respecting the Boucher case, I submit, are not applicable to the present legislation.
Another example of the supposed adequacy of the Criminal Code is section 64 and the sections immediately following, culminating with the proscription of unlawful assembly in section 67 where it requires for proof of an unlawful assembly, an assembly of three or more persons with an intent to carry out a common purpose. In order to establish guilt under this section, it is necessary to prove

that at least three people came to a meeting with a common purpose. That is not always possible to prove.
A third argument was made. This argument, I believe, raised very basic problems about the bill and whether or not, as the hon. member for Calgary North argued, it is crisis legislation. I submit it is not crisis legislation. It is problem legislation. It is not crisis legislation because it is not extreme. The hon. member for Crowfoot attempted to demonstrate how weak the bill is because of the breadth of the defences. Without agreeing with his interpretation of the bill, I say if this bill errs, it errs on the side of favouring free speech.
It is not crisis legislation in the sense that it is not stringent legislation. It is far less stringent than the Race Relations Act in Great Britain which allows no exculpation of the conduct which is condemned. It also is not crisis legislation because no one who is supporting the bill is talking about a crisis in this country. We do not have a crisis. Like most other countries in the world, we have a problem and, like most other countries in the world, we need legislation equal to that problem.
What's the problem?

The hon. member asks, "What's the problem?" I will review some of the facts set out in the committee report. The current hate campaign which that report refers to began in early 1963 and continued on to about 1966 or 1967, when it lay quiescent for a short time before it again sprang up. This campaign was carried on in eight provinces of Canada. It was perhaps carried on in the other two provinces as well but we do not have the same type of public evidence with respect to them.
I will not deal with all of the instances. They cover about four or five pages in the report of the committee. I wish first to draw to the attention of the House the situation which existed in the province of Ontario. The first distribution of hate materials began in April, 1963 in the city of Toronto. There was hate distribution in July and September. In October, there were four instances; in November five instances, and six instances in December. This was in the year 1963, before the campaign gathered momentum.
As examples of some instances of distribution of hate literature, I wish to quote examples from 1964. The report reads at page 20:
On January 15, five hundred leaflets entitled "Special Bulletin" were picked up by an apartment
April 7, 1970



administrator from tenants mailboxes in apartment houses along Don Mills Road, Victoria Park Avenue and Eglinton Avenue East in Toronto. The leaflets all had special "hate" messages typed on the reverse side.
At page 21 it reads:
On September 7 and 8, the dates of the Jewish New Year, one of the most solemn of Jewish religious holidays, a green card was received in the mail by many members of the Jewish Community in Hamilton and Toronto. The card, mailed from Toronto, depicted a Jew fleeing a large swastika, and contained the words "Thith ith the end".
On February 19, 1965, it was reported that hundreds of anti-semitic leaflets were found strewn in cars parked on the main streets and in parking lots in North Bay, Ontario. Others were reported found in the doorways of retail shops.
Some of this circulation was through the mails. Other distribution was by placing them on the streets, in shops and by hand in apartment buildings.
In Quebec there were instances of distribution in 1964 and 1965. There were instances of distribution in 1964 and 1965 in British Columbia. In Alberta, a certain amount of hate literature distribution occurred in December of 1964, in Calgary. In Saskatchewan, in April of 1965, a number of pamphlets were mailed from the Vancouver branch of Natural Order to residents of Saskatoon. In Manitoba in September of 1964, several pamphlets, including one entitled "Communism is Jewish" were mailed to the principal of a high school and others in Winnipeg.
There was distribution in New Brunswick in 1965. Pamphlets were mailed from Freder-iction, New Brunswick, to people in Moncton and Saint John. In 1964 in Nova Scotia a number of pamphlets were mailed to people in Dartmouth. This is a brief summary of the distribution of hate material contained in the report of the Special Committee on Hate Propaganda. This recital ends with the completion of the committee's work in the fall of 1965. I have not had an opportunity to complete a similar survey of all the instances of hate literature which have been distributed since that time.
I wish to refer members of the House to several other kinds of events which occurred in Toronto. After the founding of the Canadian Nazi party on April 20, 1965, these incidents occurred by way of reaction to attempts to distribute messages of hate. I will illustrate that, in matters of this kind, the reaction is something which the law has to take cognizance of as well as the actual commission of the offences under the present criminal law.

After the founding of the Nazi party in Toronto in 1965 and the setting up of a headquarters, a Nazi rally was called at Allan Gardens on Sunday, May 30. A crowd began to gather about noon, although the meeting was not called until two o'clock. By that time there were about 5,000 people in the park. When John Beattie entered the park he was immediately spotted by members of N3 Fighters Against Racial Hatred and was tackled, kicked and beaten before police could rescue him. A mob of about 500, many carrying sticks and clubs and shouting "kill, kill, kill", also chased and attacked a number of youths believed, in most cases wrongly, to be nazis. Fifty policemen eventually restored order and arrested nine men, including Beattie. Because of a lack of time, I will not go into all the difficulties which the Toronto City Council had in grappling with the problem as to whether to grant permits for meetings in the park.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
On July 25, after he had been twice denied a permit to speak in the park, Beattie and seven other nazis attempted a silent protest march through Allan Gardens carrying a swastika banner and two green maple leaf flags. As the nazi group marched into the park, two mounted policemen rode on either side. Suddenly, a small group of about 20 men jumped up from park benches, rushed the Nazis and beat them with fists and with their own flagpoles. A further incident occurred in 1966 when, as a result of a change in the park rules, Beattie was able to obtain a one-hour speaking permit for Sunday, June 5. He arrived at about 2.10 p.m. and walked through the park surrounded by police. As he began to speak, the crowd, estimated at 4,000, closed in on him, but mounted policemen pushed the spectators back and ringed Beattie for the rest of his speech. A similar meeting on Sunday, June 19, led to a near riot. Although the crowd, numbering about 1,200, was smaller than on June 5, its mood was uglier despite the presence of some 200 policemen. Beattie's halfhour speech dealt almost exclusively with Jews.
There is one further incident of this kind to which I should like to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, before coming to a conclusion. On the night of July 6, more than 1.000 angry anti-Nazi demonstrators jammed Nalhan Phillips Square in front of City Hall to denounce the city's free speech policy. He said: Mr. Speaker, in introducing the second reading of Bill C-37, I should like to preface my short remarks by saying that no current social illness is more threatening today in our country than that of drug abuse. The abuse of drugs and its consequences can be disastrous to the mental, physical, social, moral and economic health of individuals. The drug abuse problem affects not only individual drug users but also their families, friends, employers and their country. The great challenge that the drug abuse problem poses today is one which we legislators must face and to which we must also strive to find solutions.
I welcome this opportunity to bring to the attention of all hon. members Bill C-37, the purpose of which is to prohibit the publication of the name of the person so charged without special leave of the court, so that, among other things, a distinction can be made between the addict and the drug pusher.
The concept underlying this bill maintains that publishing in the newspapers the name of a person charged with possession of narcotics, including the non-narcotic drug marijuana, tends to destroy the character of the
Drug Addicts
accused, who is often a teenager. It tends to destroy the careers of students and other persons, adversely affects their families, and makes rehabilitation more difficult.
The federal government is now endeavouring to learn more about the drug abuse problem in our country by the establishment of a federal inquiry into the non-medical use of drugs. This will enable the government to learn more about the drug abuse problem so that adequate and sound legislation may be enacted as soon as possible.
In perusing literature on the drug abuse problem, statements and recommendations made by experts in this field urge lighter penalties, especially for offences relating to marijuana which should not be classified as a narcotic. Spokesmen for the Ontario Alcoholism and Drug Addiction Research Foundation have stated that, generally speaking, the creation of opportunities for lesser penalties for illegal possession as opposed to trafficking of various drug substances is a move in the right direction. It is believed by these experts that in the long run we legislators should seek to transfer drug abuse problems from the realm of criminal offences to the realm of treatable health conditions.
The traditional response whereby legal control mechanisms alone are seen as the only way to solve these problems is inadequate. I should like to quote, to prove this point, a few paragraphs contained in the brief of the Canadian Medical Association entitled "NonMedical Use of Drugs with Particular Reference to Youth", made public in November 1969:
One area of increasing agreement has emerged: the continued disdain of marijuana users for punitive legislation has forced us to re-examine the justification for and consequences of laws which treat the misuser of any drug as a criminal. Growing numbers of prominent individuals, committees and organizations are now demanding a more realistic approach, through restructuring of the drug laws, more accent on education, intensification of research, and provision of diagnostic and treatment facilities. It has become obvious that existing laws have had little influence on the spread of marijuana use and that to impose a criminal record on a young person for simple possession is self-defeating and often destructive. In Canada, within the past 12 months, many concerned groups have passed on resolutions to the federal government recommending that simple possession of marijuana be no longer treated as a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment.
The Drug Habituation Committee of the British Columbia Medical Association concluded that "the harshness of the law outweighed the probable danger of marijuana itself and that the rigid application of the law would likely give rise to social ills exceeding those inherent in the uncontrolled use of the drug itself."

A career in the professions, for example, can be lost upon conviction of this sort of thing. Therefore, it is time that we looked at all the penalties that fasten on to the non-medical use of drugs and substances like marijuana.
The bill could, of course, have been wider in scope in this sense, but I would not want in any way to oppose it since it does deal with one particular point. This point is a good place to start. This afternoon I hope that the House will give second reading to the bill, if
(Mr. Haidasz.j
only for the purpose of getting it to the committee where this problem could be examined. Mr. Speaker, I find it very difficult to consider the bill of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz), since it is so deeply related to the problems of narcotic addiction, marijuana, amphetamines, speed or what have you. I find little rationale in confining the measure to the non-publication of the names of the accused in cases dealing with narcotics.
To my mind, the principle that should be established in this bill, and I think it would be something worthy of consideration by this Parliament, is that the name of any person charged with any criminal offence should not be published until such time as that person has been convicted. If we are going to give credence to the doctrine of reasonable doubt, which applies equally to cases under the Narcotic Control Act as to the Criminal Code or any other criminal statute, that is that no one is deemed to be guilty until they have been proven so beyond a reasonable doubt, then it seems to me that no person's name should be published until after his conviction.
I think the hon. member for Parkdale is quite correct, that the mere laying of a criminal charge does a great deal to destroy the reputation and character of a person in the community. Very often the news item that the person has been charged appears, but sometimes no mention is made of the fact the person was acquitted at some subsequent date. This is particularly true when the case gets into the court of appeal after the original conviction. A bill of this nature might go a long way, if it were extended to cover all criminal offences, towards taking the sting out of charges against people when those charges are subsequently dismissed.
On many occasions it is not only the accused who suffers so far as defamation of his character is concerned. All of us who have practised in the criminal courts have seen situations where witnesses were subjected to far greater abuse than the accused himself. This can often be so in the very degrading sexual cases which we have been so unfortunate to have occur in our communities from time to time. There is nothing more difficult for a woman, the complainant in a rape case, than to be subjected to a strong and far-reaching cross-examination on the most intimate matters and the most distasteful subjects of evidence that can come before our criminal courts.
It might well be, as I suggest, that this bill would form good legislation. I am somewhat
Drug Addicts
surprised that the hon. member for Parkdale confined his remarks to young people, because the bill does in substance apply to any person, as it should. I know the hon. member has in mind the provisions of the Juvenile Delinquents Act which prohibit the publication of the names of young offenders who are processed in the juvenile courts. The report on juvenile delinquency that was prepared some years ago by the Department of Justice dealt with this particular subject and expressed the thought that this practice should not only be clarified, because it is not too clear in the present act, but that it should be extended. The report reads at page 140: Under the Act the ban on identification of the child is addressed to "newspapers and other publications". Doubt has been expressed as to whether this prohibition extends to radio and television. These doubts should be removed and the legislation should indicate clearly that identification of the child through any media whatsoever is prohibited without special leave of the court.
The hon. member for Parkdale knows that the report of the Justice Committee on Juvenile Delinquency supports the principle of his bill. What he is doing is extending it to adults. I think that is a very good thing. From time to time in our criminal courts the press have been asked by the presiding judge not to print the name of a particular witness or a particular person, and the good press of Canada have certainly obliged the judge by refraining from so doing.
I am a little concerned with the provision in the bill relating to getting special leave of the court. I cannot conceive of any situation where an accused person should have his name published if he does not wish to have it published. There are situations where it might well be that an accused person could find witnesses in his favour if his name were published. I think the bill would be better framed if it applied only to cases where the accused gave special permission.
In closing, I hope the hon. member for Parkdale will have the time to consider the bill I have pending, Bill C-154, which would also prohibit the fingerprinting of accused persons, before their conviction, under the operation of the Identification of Criminals Act. I think both in respect of my hon. friend's bill and the Identification of Criminals Act, this Parliament might well look very seriously into the way the law can, on occasions, abuse innocent persons. I look forward some time to debating more extensively those problems in respect of narcotics, but I do not believe that subject is really germane

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) is to be commended for bringing forth Bill C-37. The purpose of this bill, as stated, is to prohibit the publication of the names of the persons so charged without special leave of the court; that is, charged with possession of narcotics including marijuana. The sponsor of the bill, by profession, is a doctor. I am sure he has had wide experience in respect of the non-medical use of drugs by persons and also wide experience in respect of alcoholism. I note from clause 1 of the bill that the reference is to any person who is charged with possession. Possession certainly is the most common charge with regard to drugs. There is also, however, the charge of selling and trafficking. Experience has shown that many people charged with selling drugs or trafficking in drugs are drug addicts. Therefore, possibly this legislation does not go far enough since it does not include people who have been charged with selling drugs and trafficking in drugs. As the hon. member has stated the publication of the name can cause a great injustice in respect of the person charged and possibly, as the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hogarth) said, the witnesses who are attendant at the trial.
During the last session similar legislation was brought forward by a former member from Montreal, Mr. Klein. His bill was referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. At that time, some experts in this field gave evidence. Their evidence was excellent. I thought that possibly the government would act upon some of the recommendations made in the report of the committee in respect of that bill. Unfortunately, however, this government does not appear to want to act too quickly. We now have a situation in which many young people charged with possession of marijuana and other drugs are suffering the result of convictions when they seek employment, bonding or wish to travel. Back in the year 1966, it was said in the district of Columbia circuit court of appeals that alcoholism should be treated and not punished. That principle has been applied in some of the states of the United States. In Europe, a more enlightened view is

taken in respect of the problem of alcoholism because it is said this is really the third largest public health problem that prevails in countries today.
In Europe, and in parts of the United States, intoxication centres have been established where a person who is intoxicated is taken either by the police or by a friend. He is sobered up there and then when he has sobered up he is permitted to go home. If he should be an alcoholic he may need further treatment, and if so would be referred to another centre where he would obtain proper treatment. In other words, he is not looked upon as a criminal but as a person with an illness which should be treated. If we were to use that analogy of alcoholism in respect of the drug problem, surely we should be setting up drug centres across Canada so that a person who is in the throes of illness as a result of taking a drug could be treated before any charge is laid. As I recall the legislation proposed by Mr. Klein, it was indica'ed that when a person is charged with possession of a drug he should be brought before the magistrate. The magistrate should then suspend the hearing and either persuade the accused to take treatment voluntarily or involuntarily if necessary.
There are different types of treatment for the drug problem. Indications are that many of these have been highly successful. Once a person has been treated, then he could be returned to the court in which he had been charged. If a person were charged with possession of marijuana and it were the first offence resulting in no ill effects, surely an enlightened Crown counsel would then ask the magistrate, based on the report he received from the drug centre or hospital at which the person had been treated, to drop the charge. This would be an enlightened approach. If the report from the drug centre indicated that the person needed further treatment, and that there had been prior convictions in his case, then the charge rather than being dropped could be delayed to be brought forward at a later date, say six months, a year or even 18 months later. In other words, the case could be adjourned sine die so that the person could be further treated and tested. This is what I would like to see done, because then we would be treating the drug addict in an enlightened way. We would be treating an illness rather than punishing a person for possession of drugs.
I think all of us have known persons charged with possession of a drug who have

been convicted of the offence. The problem in respect of the RCMP and other police forces with regard to a conviction is rather difficult because possession is not the easiest thing to prove. The RCMP have been quite assiduous in pursuing the problem. The drug addict is at times most ingenious in disposing of the drug. This has put the RCMP on the alert in respect of obtaining the evidence concerning the drug charge. The result has been a growing bad relationship between the drug user and the RCMP. One would hope the relationship between the police and the person who has committed the offence would be a proper relationship. Unfortunately, as a result of this particular offence and the difficulty of obtaining the evidence necessary for a conviction, there has been a bad relationship between the police and the offender. I might say that the treatment of many young people who have been charged today with possession of marijuana has left a great deal to be desired. The result is that their attitude toward the police and law enforcement officers generally has not been a healthy one. In fact, their abuse of the police at times has been unwarranted but nevertheless they justify it because of the attitude of the law officers.

We have before us legislation concerning the obtaining of a pardon in respect of a criminal conviction. Many hon. members of the House, particularly those who sit on the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, have been disappointed with the government's bill concerning pardons for people convicted of a criminal offence. Many hon. members feel that bill should go the full way. Many are afraid of the word expungement and would prefer use of the word annulment. Be that as it may, I do not think we have gone far enough with regard to erasing the convictions of certain criminal offenders.
The Ouimet Commission recommended that any person charged with a summary offence should have the conviction erased after a period of two years, and that any person charged with an indictable offence should have the opportunity to apply for an annulment after a period of five years on proof of good behaviour and rehabilitation. The bill presented by the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcll-raith) does not go far enough.
Many high school and university students have been convicted of possession of drugs. What they did was dare to take a chance with regard to drugs, the same way as many of us in our young days dared to take a chance

with regard to alcohol. Our problem was alcohol, not drugs. Convictions against these young persons weigh heavily upon them and their prospects for future employment, bonding and travel. It is not my intention to dwell on this subject, however, Mr. Speaker.
The hon. member for New Westminster raised a question concerning the necessity of publishing the name of any person charged with a criminal offence, and suggested widening the proposed legislation to prohibit publication of offenders' names until such time as their offences had been completely dealt with by the courts and judgment passed. Mr. Speaker, it is well known that ever since my election to the House, I have always taken a special interest in the problem of the rehabilitation of prisoners and all those people who have had a run in with the law, have been found guilty, are serving time or have been released, or who have found it difficult to readjust socially and take their normal place in this world.

Besides, the family of the accused suffers needlessly. And when those people have paid their debt to society, they find it

that much more difficult to return to the outside world and contribute to the country's economy.

I will not disclose any name. Indeed, a great number of people are prosecuted, even if we are told that they are acquitted, something always remains.
