Mr. Speaker, Bill C-37 is touching on a very important question, the use of drugs, presumably by young people. The policeman is the young person's best friend, whether or not he is accepted as such, but he has a very unenviable task; he tries to protect young persons not only from themselves and their immaturity but from the worst type of criminal, the drug pusher.
Although I have the greatest sympathy for young people who fall into the drug habit, I do not know how they are to be protected unless we are pretty tough on the people making fortunes of the filthiest kind by pushing drugs to young people. I am in sympathy with the spirit of this bill which is trying to protect our young people from gaining a bad reputation and help them on the road back.
When a young person is out on a prank and is found in possession of one marijuana cigarette at a dance or some such place, perhaps the law is a little overeager in wanting a conviction at the present time. This is just the smallest link in the chain of conspiracy of the unhealthy and very serious drug racket. We have to be careful about who we are trying to protect, and the bill must be specific in this respect. When the bill says "any person", surely it does not mean a man already convicted of several offences of pushing drugs. Surely it does not mean a young person who has been given a suspended sentence, allowed to return to his normal routine and later found to be passing drugs in large quantities. Are we to believe that we are trying to protect such people? Perhaps I am being technical, but I think the bill should specify exactly who we are trying to protect and under what circumstances.
April 7, 1970

[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The person caught smoking his first marijuana cigarette should certainly be protected with regard to publication of his name.
I doubt whether any magistrate, if it was within his power, would do anything except put a boy like that on suspended sentence or remand him in the custody of his parents with the understanding that if no more drugs were found nothing more would be heard of the matter. I hope that in cases like these the press will use discretion and keep the name of the boy out of print. Certainly, if the long arm of the law catches the pusher or the person helping him, I would not expect the press to extend the same discretion.
The bill does not mention age. I suggest there should be a great difference in the way boys of 16 and under are treated and the way boys between 16 and 18 are treated. Any person older than 19 years-after all, we say these days that boys of 18 ought to assume their civic responsibilities-should experience the full rigour of the law. The law should deal very severely with persons of 18 or 19 years of age who ought to know that pushing drugs on young people in this country and elsewhere is a very serious offence indeed.
I do not think we need look abroad and see what is happening in other countries, although it is interesting to note that in several countries the offence of drug pushing carries the death penalty. In those countries the sale and use of drugs has dropped off dramatically. This includes drugs such as marijuana. Whether marijuana is a dangerous drug, I do not know, although I notice the bill lumps all drugs together. I am thinking mainly of marijuana in my presentation. The evidence about this drug is conflicting. I am not at all sure, Mr. Speaker, the possession of more serious, hard narcotics is a matter that should be treated lightly. I think the bill should spell out whether possessors of marijuana should be treated differently from possessors of hard drugs.
The person possessing a drug may be the only link in a long chain leading back to the drug trafficker who is really dangerous to our society. I would go along with any method of protecting the reputation of young people who for the first time have innocently come into contact with drugs. Even if charged, their names and addresses ought to be withheld, at least until the time of the trial. I do not think such young people ought to have their names smeared unnecessarily. If a person is convicted, that is different. Boys

falling within the age limits I referred to ought to be protected, even if they are convicted. On the other hand, when the pusher of drugs is apprehended, the more publicity given to his being engaged in this most notorious of trades, the better. On this point I cannot go along with the spirit of the bill.
I agree with the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) who suggests the bill is very important and ought to be referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. Expert witnesses could be called. I should like to see witnesses from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police drug squad called. They are responsible for protecting our young people and could give guidance as to how we might protect them from using drugs on the campuses, on the beaches and elsewhere. If there were liaison between our young people and the ROMP and our young people realized that the ROMP wish to protect them, we might be more successful in tracking down drug traffickers who are the real criminal element in our society and who must be apprehended as soon as possible.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words with respect of arguments adduced by my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Roberts), with respect to the amendment and to the bill. My colleague said that the thrust of liberalism over the centuries has been toward liberty. I agree of course that the thrust of liberalism has been toward liberty. But liberalism is not a one-sided philosophy; it is for equality and security as well as liberty. Indeed, it might be argued that the very purpose of liberty is to enable the achievement of equality and security in our society.
My colleague quoted the great liberal philosopher John Stuart Mill to the effect that legislation should be enacted only when there is a situation that transgresses specific and identifiable rights. I submit that is precisely the situation before us. We have specific and identifiable human rights which are being

transgressed. These rights have not been previously recognized by law. That is the purpose of this change which is being made in the law. The offence of group defamation is one which has not been recognized by law until now. This is a new law which will recognize this human right. It is not a sacred cow, as my colleague suggested; it is a sacred right of the people of this country.
My colleague also suggested that the effect of this bill would be to drive hatred and hatemongers underground. If that were the case, I submit the purpose of this bill would be fully achieved. This bill is not aimed at thought; it is aimed at speech and conduct, especially speech which goes toward unlawful conduct. If we could succeed in driving hate and hatemongers underground, we would succeed in ridding the democratic dialogue of our country of this cancer.
This bill is aimed at establishing minimal standards for public debate. I stress the word "minimal". It is not a bill specifically aimed at protecting either the minority or majority group in our society. In practice it will undoubtedly normally protect the minority because the minority, as the weaker members of our society, comprises usually the groups which are attacked. Occasionally it may succeed in protecting the majority. This does not disturb me. If members of the minority behave in such a fashion that they depart from the minimum standards of debate which we believe are necessary in this country in order to protect the interest of groups-not the interest of the government but the interests of citizens in our society who can be attacked by reason of their group membership-or if members of either minority or majority fall afoul of this new legislation, so be it. The purpose of the legislation will be achieved if we achieve minimal standards of public debate which eliminate the dregs of discussion, discussion which would spew forth hatred at groups.
In my opinion this bill represents a great step forward in the law. It represents a new sophistication which deals with an old problem which we have newly realized, one of great social dimensions. I support the bill. I cannot support the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-3. We have before us in this House a bill which is still more tangible evidence of the direction in which we are being led by the present orientated government. We have still more evidence that any legislation

presented by this government must steer across the board and encompass, not only the actions of all citizens but thoughts and
statements that are a substance of a free society.
I cannot accept the view put forward by the government that Bill C-3 is a necessary piece of legislation. Like any other reasonable, compassionate individual, and as a representative of the people in our Parliament, I put myself on record as being in favour of any effort by any individual or group that would promote good will. I would heartily support any effort to remove from our society the causes of hatred and distrust. Mr. Speaker, I would even go so far as to endorse the spirit of this bill in so far as it makes it a crime to advocate the extinction of any group or segment of our society because of race, colour or for any reason. I do not believe that any group in this country is in danger of extinction by genocide, but I would be willing to erect any reasonable safeguards that would ensure that this could never happen here.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
It is a paradox, Mr. Speaker, that the only real requirement for legislation such as Bill C-3 would be to protect the people and the very Parliament in which we sit against encroachments by the government that proposed Bill C-3. Our society is made up of individuals first of all. Any measures designed to protect groups within a society must take into account that the individual is paramount. Our fundamental and basic concern for the individual did not come about by chance or accident. It was bought at great price and sacrifice by all the generations that came before us. It was bought with the efforts and the pains and the ministrations of our founding families. It was bought with the blood of our patriots. And it has been tempered with the wisdom of past generations of great Canadian parliamentarians. In short, Mr. Speaker, the preservation of the sovereignty of the individual might be called our principal reason for being.
I would be the first to agree that society, any society, must have form and body and substance. I would be the first to agree that it would be impossible for any society to survive in an acceptable form if it did not recognize the requirement for order and for protection of the rights of citizens from conspirators and demagogues. However, Mr. Speaker, within the framework of an orderly and lawful society we must also have the
Hate Propaganda
greatest possible guarantees, within reasonable bounds, that the rights of the individual will remain the paramount consideration of government. I would add here that the principal task of the opposition in this Parliament is to guard against incursions on individual rights by our present government.
Bill C-3 in its present form is far too restrictive and its wording is open to too many interpretations. This makes the intent of the bill too restrictive and far too punitive. I want to come back to that point later, the part of the bill that lends itself to such a loose interpretation of peace officers and jurists.
I mentioned that the intent of this bill is too restrictive; there are insidious overtones in it which should not be taken lightly. When laws are too restrictive, when laws are too oppressive, it becomes impossible for the individual to fit comfortably into his environment. The best way to encourage contempt for the law is to make laws which show contempt for the individual. In such situations the laws are often disregarded and in time patterns of contempt for the law will develop. When laws are too rigidly imposed and too rigidly enforced, the individual will strive to break out of his oppressive environment and revolutions are born.
I would like to return to what I called the intent of this bill, or at least the intent which is implied in the government's wording of it. The intent of the wording would appear to be a desire on the part of the government to venture into the realm of moral legislation or, more explicitly, of legislating morality. This is a strange turnabout when one recalls the insistence of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) just a year ago that the government was not interested in or concerned with the morals of the individual Canadian. I should like to quote from an editorial which appeared in today's Globe and Mail, as follows:
"The problem of trying to render synonymous law and morality is that we then come down to the question: Whose morality? Whose standards of behaviour? Whose sense of morality? Who is to determine the standard? Who is to attribute blame? Who is to say what is moral and immoral? Who is to decide when moral responsibility exists in terms of freedom of will, and when it has to be diluted in human terms because of environmental or physical causes?... In a pluralistic society there may be different standards, differing attitudes, and the law cannot reflect them all. Public order, in this situation of a pluralistic society, cannot substitute for private conduct. We believe that morality is a matter for private conscience. Criminal law should reflect the public order only."

Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to support the amendment before the House if only because it emasculates the bill, which I think is the only way to treat the bill. Unlike some members who have spoken against the bill and see it as a dangerous, bad bill, I do not feel that strongly about the dangers that are inherent in it. I do not see the bill having any serious effect in regard to limiting freedom of speech in our society. My own feeling is that the courts will lean over backwards to make sure that justice is done and that the benefit of the doubt is given to those people who appear before them. Having said that, a person is not in a position to know how a judge will react or how the courts generally over the years will change.
From experience in society I would not think that freedom of speech would be seriously limited by the bill. My reasons for so saying are different from those of others who have spoken. My reasons are that the bill is really an impossible bill, that it is a foolish bill. It is all too easy to dismiss the problem of hatred by passing legislation. It is all too easy to pretend that we can cope with this serious situation in society simply by passing a piece of legislation after which everybody goes home and feels great, that they have done something about hatred, that they have struck a blow against hatred. This is an illusion, and one nobody should be under.
As a layman looking at the law, I see three general categories. One is the kind of law that everybody agrees must be passed because it is required for the safety of society. We must have laws to deal with murder, to regulate traffic, and so on, because society just cannot exist without them. Such laws meet with almost universal acceptance. This is really their strength; everybody in society agrees that these laws are necessary, and people give up part of their freedom in return for greater freedom as a result of the protection accorded them under these laws.
The second category of laws governs such things as fair employment and discrimination as it concerns housing. These laws are not 100 per cent effective and are frequently evaded. But they do serve a purpose. People in society state how they feel about these things, and to
Hate Propaganda
a large extent these laws are enforced, though not completely, because they are definite and specific and apply to particular situations.
We then come to the third kind of laws, laws that try to legislate morality. Experience in society shows that you cannot legislate morality. I see no evidence that we have ever been able to legislate morality. I suggest the law we are discussing here is this kind of law: it attempts to provide that people shall like each other, that people shall not say unkind or hateful things about other people.
Morality is a very difficult subject to deal with. First of all, morality changes from one time to another time. What is considered immoral at one stage may not be considered immoral later. There is also the question of definition. How do you define pornography- though I know we have attempted to? How would you define hatred, when you really get down to it?
My views are very subjective and I must admit are much influenced by my personal experience. My personal experience tells me a number of things. I am not unfamiliar with prejudice. I am not unfamiliar with how shattering hatred in society can be. During the war I had a chance to see the ultimate, fearful results of hatred. I was in Belsen very soon after the camp was taken by the allies, and the visible evidence was there to see. I wonder whether a hate literature bill would have prevented that sort of thing. I do not believe it would. I do not think that any hate literature legislation could have prevented the sort of thing that happened at that time.
On the other hand, I am also very fortunate, in observing how society has developed in my own time, to see how much progress we in Canada have made on the question of tolerance of one group by another. We live in a much changed society today. Our society is much different from the one I knew as a boy. Why is this so? After all, there were no hate literature bills during the last 20 or 30 years, yet these changes have taken place. They have taken place because of the lot of the people; their situation has improved tremendously. The causes of hatred have declined. The sort of things hatred feeds on have started to disappear; and this is really where hatred must be tackled. As a socialist, I feel that this is the only way we can abolish hatred. There cannot be freedom or security for any minority group unless there is freedom and security for everybody in society. But this cannot be rushed or hurried, and it seems to me that passing this sort of legislation is a grave error.

As I said earlier, I do not think this legislation is dangerous, but I do fear complacency. With this legislation on the books, people in society will pretend to themselves that they have done something about the problem when in fact this is not the case; they have simply diverted their eyes from the problem. That is the greatest danger posed by this kind of legislation: it will prevent our coming to grips with the real causes of hatred and dissatisfaction in our society, and this is the real issue.
I know that we live in a very squeamish kind of society. We do not like to see ugliness around us. We apply a cosmetic to ugliness and pretend that it is not there. We try to push it out of the way, and this approach is very dangerous. It is better to see the ugliness fully exposed, where we can deal with it, than shove it off in some corner or paint it over with make-up, powder or rouge so that it looks prettier than it really is.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
We do a disservice to our society if we pretend that hatred and discrimination do not exist. My plea is for realism and for acknowledgement that these difficulties are still with us and have to be dealt with. I do not want to see anything done that will obscure the real diseases of our society. I am not interested in making people feeling more confortable. I want them to feel uncomfortable; I want them to be confronted by and to see this ugliness, rather than have it hidden. I am very worried that we will not get rid of hate literature simply by passing this legislation. What we will do is make it more subtle and perhaps more pallatable. Maybe we will stop it here and there and people will not be so terribly offended. But nothing really will be solved by doing this.
I think there is an increasing danger that the indefinable thing that we may call tradition or good will, which does not depend on the law but is part of our society-sympathy, if you will-will be lost to those suffering from hatred and will tend to support those disseminating hatred under the false notion that they are defending freedom of speech and the right of even the most vile minorities to be heard. There is this danger.
I want to speak from personal experience. I have been through numerous political campaigns. I do not think I have ever been in a political campaign where hate literature in one form or another was not used against me. Always my party worker would come to me with a piece of literature or a story that was

being spread around and say, "We have to bash this on the head and wade right into it. We have to stop it." I have always said, "No, because you cannot stop it." They have asked, "What is going to happen?" and I have always replied, "If people want to believe this sort of nonsense, this kind of junk, this scurrilous stuff being spread around, nothing you or I can do will make any difference. We have only one hope, that the people will see it for what it is. If they do not see it for what it is, we are lost anyway and what do you accomplish?" Either there is an element of decency, fair-mindedness and intelligence in society, or the ball game is lost anyway. You have to count on that. This approach has always worked and the element of decency and intelligence has been there.
In the last campaign, in 1968, all of us were aware of the kind of hate literature that was being circulated against the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). It was dreadful stuff. On the whole I think it helped to get him elected. I know that during the course of the campaign my party workers came to me with this literature and asked whether I was going to let these things be said, even though they were being said about an opponent. They would ask if I was going to take advantage of the situation. I repeatedly, during my campaign, had to divert from my own rather urgent need to consolidate my position and take a stand against hate literature because it offended the decency and intelligence of my people. We wanted to beat the opponent, but we did not want to beat him that way. The Prime Minister probably gained a measure of sympathy that he would not have gained had this literature not been spread around.
What do we gain by banning the worst forms of ugliness contained in such literature? We feel a little more comfortable-but is it worth it? Isn't it better to have it where you can see it and deal with it, where you can appeal to the intelligence of people? You can ask whether they are going to listen to this kind of stuff. You can ask whether it is not offensive to them. I would rather do it that way, and I think in the long run that is the way to do it.
I appreciate the feelings of people who have been discriminated against, particularly those who were subjected to the extreme form of discrimination found in concentration camps. You cannot expect them to be politically objective, perhaps the way I am trying to be at this moment, about hate literature. When they see something like this they are
April 7, 1970

reminded that it is not just an occurrence during an election campaign; it is an indication that their lives may be in danger. It is understandable that they would press the government and society to afford them some protection which would relieve them of the haunting fear of this recurring menace.
The question that must be asked is. Do we have to succumb to that plea, as legitimate as their fears may be? In some ways those who are looking for protection from hate literature may find that their insecurity is heightened as a result of the passage of this bill. Every nut, every crackpot and every lunatic will now have the opportunity of testing this legislation in court. They will seek prosecution so they can have their day in court. The type of person who is disposed of by the newspapers and the other news media have been discounted for what they are. They will now have the sympathy of the editorial pages. I would add that the editorial pages are unwisely and unnecessarily sympathetic, but that is the way of editorial pages. Every one of these people will now be able to be part of a cause celebre. If a court should sentence them to jail, they will come out martyrs. This will give them a status they do not deserve. It will give them a position to which they are not entitled. There is some danger in this approach and we have to be very concerned about it.
I made these brief remarks because I felt someone like myself should make them. I conclude by saying that in the final analysis the safety of minorities depends upon the good sense and the security of our whole society. You cannot protect minorities unless you change society and protect all of society.

Mr. Speaker, I shall speak but briefly on Bill C-3, if only to put on record that basically I consider it an unnecessary piece of legislation. I know of no minority group that is prejudiced by our social system as it exists today. I know of no threat to any minority group in our nation. If such existed I could readily understand the need for the passage of such legislation.
In a free society such as ours we can do anything that the law does not make illegal. Even the minister has not demonstrated the need for such legislation. He did say that the legislation would show the world our good intentions. I find it very unusual that we have to amend the Criminal Code to show the world that we have such intentions. It is idle to suggest that this legislation will prevent the commission of such crimes in the future.

The existence of the legislation may do more harm than good in drawing attention to the possible existence of such crimes in our free society.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
The great test of this legislation will come, say, in ten years from now. If one looks back over such a period and finds no convictions, so much the better. But it will more than anything else show the lack of need of such legislation at this time. It is also difficult to understand the Attorney General being appointed the watchdog of this legislation any more than in respect of the other sections of the Criminal Code. Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to become involved in what I believe to be a very significant piece of legislation. In the first instance I wish to say I reject the amendment put forward by my own colleague. In keeping with my conscience, it would nullify the principle of the bill. The bill strikes at that which is of extreme importance, that is, the incitement or promotion of hatred. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I accept the bill in its entirety. I do not find it offensive, untimely or particularly dangerous.
I am not here to become involved in the niceties of the legal matters in respect of this bill, because I believe sincerely that all legislation no matter whether it stems from this House or from any other place is subject to comment regarding its workability. For some time I was a member of the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. The members of the committee were sincerely concerned with the bill in the first place, as I was and still am, and attempted to make to that bill the amendments they believed were necessary in order to make it workable.
If this bill should pass, of course it will be for the courts to give their judicial interpretation of a matter to which we have given deep and sensible deliberation. I am very concerned about the bill, but at the same time I appreciate the varied views of my colleagues. It seems to me there has been one theme running through the entire debate. Everyone seems to be for the principle of the bill-but! This "but" which continually came before me

really had me concerned, because I cannot see how one can be so emphatic about being for the principle of the bill and then say "but".
I do not know whether the bill is perfect. Perhaps it is not perfect. Maybe it is contrary to the thinking of some of us. It may, on the other hand, be shocking. We as Canadians and parliamentarians must discuss this type of legislation. Perhaps this legislation would not have been necessary had we followed, as I indicated in my maiden speech, the advice of one Adele Florence Corey. I should like to quote from Hansard of September 20, 1968- but remember that when I first spoke in this House I was more nervous than I am now. As recorded at page 291 of Hansard for September 20, 1968, I mentioned what this woman had said a long time ago. I said:
She said that men should be judged not by the colour oi their skin nor by the way they fight, love or sin, nor by the gods they serve or vintage they drink, but by the quality of the thoughts they think.
Hear, hear!

If mankind were prepared to accept that very simple principle, we would not have my friend stating earlier that in his wisdom he thinks we are wasting time because we would not have to be discussing this bill. But, Mr. Speaker, some people will not accept the principle I have just enunciated. It is not within their thinking. It is not within their moral fibre to accept that principle. I do not know whether there are many faults in this bill, but with all its alleged faults and with all the shortcomings that were expressed this evening and yesterday I sincerely state that it is a step in the right direction. It offers hope to the many people who have long suffered, the many people who have long been humiliated, and the many people who have long been ignored.
This bill offers hope in that it is an indication that someone is aware of the problem that actually exists, that someone is aware that inciting hatred toward identifiable groups is unacceptable. I ask this simple question: Is it good just to have this type of reasoning? We are concerned about a particular condition and we say it is unacceptable. Is this in keeping with our democratic principles? I suggest that what we are now doing, and have been doing for the past two days is good and is in keeping with the principles of democracy. Hate as expressed by some Canadians in our midst concerns me, and it concerned the Cohen committee. I should like IMr. Alexander.]
to read from pages 25 and 24 of the report of the special committee:
In the committee's view the "hate" situation in Canada, although not alarming, clearly is serious enough to require action. It is far better for Canadians to come to grips with this problem now, before it attains unmanageable proportions, rather than deal with it at some future date in an atmosphere of urgency, of fear and perhaps even of crisis. The Canadian community has a duty, not merely the right, to protect itself from the corrosive effects of propaganda that tends to undermine the confidence that various groups in a multicultural society must have in each other. The committee therefore concludes that action by government is necessary-
Let me revert to page 24:
The number of organizations involved and the numbers of persons hurt is no test of the issue: the arithmetic of a free society will not be satisfied with oversimplified statistics demonstrating that few are casting stones and not many are receiving hurts. What matters is that incipient malevolence and violence, all of which are inherent in "hate" activity, deserves national attention.
Not local, but national attention.
However small the actors may be in number, the individuals and groups promoting hate in Canada constitute "a clear and present danger" to the functioning of a democratic society. For in times of social stress such "hate" could mushroom into a real and monstrous threat to our way of life.
Therefore, the committee was concerned-a committee set up by Parliament. Hence this bill. Our fathers and our grandfathers, responsible as they were in their day, were also irresponsible. They were irresponsible for projecting and being preoccupied with notions of their fellowman, all based on myths-the Jew, the black man, people of colour and those whose names ended in "i" or "o". That was their way of life, Mr. Speaker. That was how things were done then. But it is changed now. Those types of attitudes are no longer acceptable. I believe that the thinking Canadian has been awakened by the truths slashing away at the myths, truths about hate, and he has gathered this information from the media in all forms. Because, Mr. Speaker, it is my considered opinion that hate disrupts our social, economic and political orders and structures and, most important, it can be extremely expensive. That, I know, has been brought home to us on many occasions in the past few years.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I believe the vast majority of Canadians will accept the principle of this bill, as many members here do, except when they say "but". The Canadian people will accept the principle of this bill notwithstanding the
April 7. 1970

editorials and the lobbies. There is in Canada now a concerned generation that is aware of attitudes that can lead to no good as far as the ultimate destiny of Canada is concerned.
Let me refer again to the Cohen committee report, page 67:
The history of law and opinion as concurrent developments is replete with instances, as A. V. Dicey long ago indicated, not only where law reflected the state of opinion but where a fluid opinion was itself crystallized by law. This generation of Canadians is more sensitive to the dangers of prejudice and vicious utterances than ever before. Such public opinion, therefore, should now be prepared to crystallize these sensitivities, fears and doubts into positive statements of self-protecting policy-namely statements of law.
Statements of law, Mr. Speaker! This bill is not the first of its type. In Ontario we have the Ontario Human Rights Code, a codification of all acts on discrimination dating back to 1944, passed in code form in 1962 and administered by the Ontario Human Rights Commission. Let me read the preamble of the Ontario Human Rights Code, which I think all Canadians are interested in and in which they should be interested:
Whereas recognition of the inherent dignity and the equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family is the foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world and is in accord with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as proclaimed by the United Nations:
And whereas it is public policy in Ontario that every person is free and equal in dignity and rights without regard to race, creed, colour, nationality, ancestry or place of origin-
Such a preamble is equally applicable to the nation, Mr. Speaker. We have other such acts in our great land. This is not the first time an act has come before parliamentarians that had to do with conduct and attitudes. We have federal legislation such as the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. Listen to a list of the provinces that are involved with all sorts and types of human rights legislation: Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and Saskatchewan.
In the past two days we have been discussing guidelines for human behaviour as it affects man. This bill points out that which is unacceptable to the Canadian way of life. It is not a code for love. That is the red herring that is always thrown into this type of argument, that you cannot legislate love. No one wants anyone else to love them when it comes to this type of legislation. It is a code directed towards conduct, towards overt action. I respectfully state that the greatest 22218-
Hate Propaganda
force that should exist today is man's relentless pursuit of the attainment of better human relations between all peoples.
Hear, hear!

But how do you do it, Mr. Speaker? It has been said that you start in the home. Well, how long have we heard this? Mom is supposed to teach junior to respect his fellow friend. Then when you cannot get it through the home, they tell you to go to the church. I do not want to get into the area of the church, but they say, "Go to church. The church will help you." When that fails they say we are supposed to have group discussions. When that fails then they say, "Leave it to education." I have heard all these things running through the debate all afternoon. Then, Mr. Speaker, last but not least we come to legislation. When all else fails with the good intentions of mankind and with the background man professes to have in Christian love and brotherly love, and that cannot arrive at the necessary solutions, I respectfully state it is my public duty as a parliamentarian to start thinking about legislation. .
Hear, hear!

That is why, Mr. Speaker, I do not know who is for this bill on the outside, but I am not particularly worried. I am not thinking of it as a politician, as a Progressive Conservative, or as a Liberal in the way that we have heard some hon. members talk. I am thinking about this problem as a man whose conscience is being affected, as a man who has some awareness of what it means to be a member of a minority group.
You cannot legislate love, nor can you legislate against prejudice. But, Mr. Speaker, surely you can legislate against the overt act of discrimination. I do not know whether this bill will work, but I hope it will. It can work in this area, in that it is a form of education. But it is a form of education the hard way. We could not get it the easy way, so we had to do it the hard way.
In the committee I listened to a discussion on the possibility of this bill backfiring on those it is attempting to protect. I got into the debate, into the questioning on that matter, because if this was a fact I did not want any part of the bill. I know the interaction, that is becoming more and more a part of our way of life, by those who are attempting to show society the wrongs that they have been affected by over the years. But I was advised, Mr. Speaker, that the minority striving for recog-

April 7, 1970
Hate Propaganda
nition, proclaiming their desire to become a real force in the mainstream of Canadian life rather than accepting misery in their insignificant tributaries, would be protected by the defences that were eventually written into the bill. But I believe, too, that the defences are also open to those who proclaim that freedom of speech is being affected. Mr. Speaker, all I can say is that I believe-this is just my considered opinion-the defences therein equally can protect freedom of speech. All I know is that when you start talking about freedom of speech and freedom of the press, sooner or later the dignity of man, the value of man, transcends freedom of speech and these matters must be protected by society.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I do not know what the experience of my colleagues who speak about Bill C-3 has been, but I reflect on the name-calling, the frustrations, the rejections, the spite and the hate that have occurred in my life. I have been fortunate, but let me tell you that there are a lot of people not so fortunate. I do not want to point to any particular province but it does not take much imagination to think of the east. I know a little about the black man's position because I am black and proud of it. He has been abused; he has been confused.
Mr. Speaker, what does a mother say to her child who comes running home crying because his skin is black, or cries when he goes to bed at night because he is a member of a minority group? Does she tell him that freedom of speech is paramount? What does a father say to his family when, as a result of hatred and contempt, he cannot bring home bread in order to sustain life? I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker, with illustrations that would frighten a lot of people in terms of what hatred can mean, and how frustration can lead the people affected by it to believe that they are inferior and have no rights within society because those who are bigoted use hate propaganda to the extent that a man becomes possessed and believes it to be true.
What we are doing here is creating an atmosphere not out of crisis but out of a new awareness of what hatred could do to Canada. I should like to read from the Ontario Human Rights Code something which illustrates what I mean by creating an atmosphere. This was printed in 1967, and God knows it is applicable in 1970! On the back of the book is this statement:
The aim of Ontario's Human Rights Code is to create at the community level a climate of under-

standing and mutual respect, in which all our people of whatever racial, religious or cultural background-new Canadian no less than native bom-will be made to feel that all are equal in dignity and rights, that each is a part of the whole Canadian community, and that each has a rich contribution to make to the development and well being of our province and nation. Few will disagree that this is a prerequisite for the building of a truly healthy Canadianism.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion I say that in my humble opinion Bill C-3 is a prerequisite of this mood, leading to a truly healthy Canadianism.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in view of the speeches made today I think it a great pity that the rather disturbed young man who was in the gallery yesterday did not have the opportunity of hearing them. There have been many fine speeches on both sides of the House which have completely crossed party lines. Had he heard them, he might have had a different view of the purpose of this institution.
Hear, hear!

I might add that I hope the press gives the same prominence to some of the speeches made today as it did to the unfortunate and ill-informed remarks of that young man yesterday.
I think it is quite clear that there is not any member of this House in any party who does not agree with the principles and objectives of this bill. The only disagreement is on the means of attaining these ends. The objections seem to lie largely in one of the many sections of the bill, namely section 267A subsections 1, 2 and 3.
In this respect I think the bill is badly drafted because it not only attains the objectives that we all have in mind, but a few that were not intended, as has been ably pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) and other members on both sides of the House. This is what really concerns the members and it is the reason for the debate continuing as long as it has. Some of us are very much afraid that not only will the commendable and excellent objectives pointed out by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) be attained, but others less desirable will also be attained. We are always accused of wasting the time of the House by repeating arguments. I do not want to be guilty of that, although I feel that section 267A may create situations never contemplated when the bill was drafted.
April 7, 1970

I have another reason for wanting to speak on this bill. Other members have not hesitated to blow their own horns in this debate, so I should not hesitate to say that several years ago I was one of the first members to bring this matter before the House of Commons in a private bill. Other members, some of whom are still here, also brought it before the House. Apparently the government of the day did take some notice of members with private bills, the Cohen commission was established and today we have this bill before us.
I should like to deal in some detail with the bill which I introduced at that time. It might be helpful if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) would take some notice of it. He never seems to take much notice of suggestions, but perhaps he would this time. The second time I put my private bill on the Order Paper it was Bill C-164 of the first session of the twenty seventh Parliament and appeared on April 4, 1966. I had consulted the legal adviser of this House, a gentleman with wide legal knowledge, Dr. Ollivier. I had suggested putting in a bill all by itself, but he advised me to present it as an amendment to the Criminal Code. The bill that I presented at that time had two clauses. They are very brief and I should like to put them on the record because I think they may be very helpful in this debate. The first clause reads as follows:
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Subsection (1) of section 248 of the Criminal Code is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
'248.(1) A defamatory libel is matter published, *without lawful justification or excuse, that is likely to injure the reputation of any person by exposing him to hatred, contempt or ridicule, or that is designed to insult the person of or concerning whom it is published or that is likely to injure the reputation of any group of persons by exposing them as a group to hatred, contempt or ridicule by reason of their racial or national origin, colour, or religion, or that is designed to insult any group of persons by reason of their racial or national origin, colour, or religion.'
The explanatory note to the bill at that time was as follows:
This bill proposes to enlarge the Criminal Code definition of a defamatory libel, to include 'hate literature'. Because such literature is, in many cases, the expression of a sick mind, the bill further proposes that any person charged or convicted of publishing such a libel shall be placed under mental observation to determine whether he is mentally ill.
Before I read the second clause of the bill I should like particularly to note the remarks made this evening by the hon. member for
Hate Propaganda
Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) who, along with other hon. members, took very much the same view I have taken, that those who promote hate literature and defamatory group libel are sick people and ought properly to be treated as such. At the time I introduced the bill originally, a series of rather indecorous events had taken place in the city of Toronto. A young man-I will not dignify his name by repeating it in this House-was creating racial disturbances. His attacks were aimed against the Hebrew people particularly in the city of Toronto. Because the authorities were using various methods in an attempt to prevent this, the lad became something of a martyr with some of the low-minded, the sick-minded and the ignorant. He became the object of praise and a leader, just as was Adolph Hitler at one time in Nazi Germany, as some can well remember. I think the hon. member for Waterloo put it very well: we do not want to make martyrs of these kinds of people.
Some years ago I had the opportunity, as had the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hogarth), of being a Crown attorney. I well remember an incorrigible young man who kept appearing in the police court in my area. He was a repeater, and was charged with every kind of petty, and sometimes more serious offence. No one knew how to deal with him. He was sent to reformatory and came back a hero. His time inside his friends thought of as you think of chevrons on a sleeve. Every time he went to prison he attained a sort of good conduct stripe as far as his buddies were concerned.
After a little thought it was decided he would not be such a popular hero if he were treated as if he were ill and sent to the Ontario Hospital for observation. The strange thing is this: it seems that when people come out of that institution, to which they are sent when their behaviour is such that they may be retained as a guest for some time, they come out not as heroes but as objects of ridicule. That is exactly what happened in this case. My experience in this matter rather prompted the drafting of the second clause in the bill I presented at that time. It reads as follows:
The said act is amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 251 thereof, the following:
'251A. Where a defendant is alleged to have published a libel defamatory of a group of persons within the meaning of subsection (1) of section 248, the court, judge, justice or magistrate may at any stage of the proceedings remand the defendant, by order in writing, to such custody as the court, judge, justice or magistrate directs for oh-

April 7, 1970
Hate Propaganda
servation for a period not exceeding thirty days to determine whether the defendant is mentally ill; and where the defendant is not so remanded and is found guilty, the court, judge, justice or magistrate shall so remand the defendant before sentence.
I think that if a provision such as this had been included in the present hate literature bill there would be no danger of making heroes out of hate peddlers. There would be no danger of giving these people a lot of publicity if they were sent for a mental examination, which is what they ought to have. They would not come out of hospital and be heroes for the drug store-corner gang any longer; they would be objects of ridicule and contempt. To make the punishment fit the crime, I can think of nothing better for them. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, in my rather brief experience I have found this sort of thing works.
I know other hon, members wish to speak, and I do not wish to take up more time than is necessary. I think new section 267A, subsections 1, 2 and 3, may very well defeat the purpose of the bill. I think those subsections will accomplish a number of purposes we have in mind but, as I have already said, they may accomplish other much less desirable purposes.
This debate has crossed party lines. It is not becoming a party issue in this House. The cabinet may not think so, but the backbenchers on all sides of the House do. I think the Minister of Justice and his advisers might very well withdraw the bill temporarily, look at its drafting, pay attention to some of the suggestions which have been made in this House, and perhaps consider redrafting this clause so as to accomplish the purposes of the bill without leaving the loopholes which have been pointed out, which might endanger free speech and all the other things we have heard about. I hope the government does this.
One cannot impute motives to the bill, and very properly so, because no one really knows what is going on inside somebody else's brain. If the government refuses to pay attention to the suggestions made here, one can only assume that the reason for introducing the bill is that suggested by one hon. member, that it is presented largely for political purposes. It was given a great deal of windowdressing, trumpeting and fanfare, but it is clear that the same objectives could have been achieved by a simple amendment to the Criminal Code. The Minister of Justice is always telling us he wants to make further amendments to that document. If he had done 
just that in a simple way, without all these trappings, I think everyone would have appreciated it very much more and the amendment could have accomplished these ends.
I have found one thing a little unconvincing in the remarks of the Minister of Justice and one or two other hon. members of the House. When the Criminal Code amendments were before the House and we were considering controversial matters such as abortion, homosexuality and other things, there were many high-flown speeches saying that you cannot legislate morals and that morality does not come under the criminal law. That was how some talked out of one side of their mouths at that time.
Yesterday and today we heard similar arguments about the purposes of this legislation, but exactly the reverse arguments were used, namely, that morality does come under the criminal law, that this bill may point the way to how people should behave, that it may give guidelines to human conduct and all the rest of it. I find this peculiar double-standard of reasoning very hard to take. I am one member of this House who does not think morality can be legislated. I have never thought so from the first day I entered law school and had the benefit of the opinions of some eminent people in that regard, including the former Chief Justice who has just retired.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I find it difficult to understand why people with considerable experience in the legal profession argue that morality can be legislated on one occasion and not on another. It is for this reason I find some of the arguments put forward in favour of the bill a little difficult to comprehend.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say I am in favour of the principle of the bill.
I think every hon. member in this House is in favour of it. However, I think the two sections to which I have referred should be redrafted. While I agree they may well accomplish the purposes of this bill, I fear they may also accomplish other objectionable purposes and open the door to those with evil intent who would twist the law for their own evil purposes, as we have often seen done in this country and in many other places. As I have said, I hope the Minister of Justice will pay attention to the many fine arguments put forward from both sides of the House.

Mr. Speaker, hate propaganda is an extremely important
April 7, 1970

subject. I am one who believes that you cannot fight hatred with hatred. That may sound strange coming from a man who spent most of life enforcing laws, some of them fierce but most of them humane. Although I am not particularly proud of a part of my life, I would do it again. I refer to the seven years I spent fighting the nazi regime in Germany. If we are to believe all that we hear, the nazi regime in Germany committed one of the most savage acts of race annihilation in modern times. I suppose if by legislation we were able to prevent that type of thing, we would be unanimous in supporting such legislation.
I do not think that any legislation can put down hatred-on the contrary. I do not think harsh laws reduce hatred. It is strange that in this Parliament when we are liberalizing the law pretty well across the board, we are rushing into a permissive society. In some circles it is no longer thought evil to peddle drugs to our young people. It is certainly not considered evil to partake of them. It is strange that we should suddenly find it necessary to put something into the Criminal Code which has been tolerated for a thousand years. In fact, it has been more than tolerated: it was fought for with all the vigour which it was possible to produce by the fearless island people and their descendants, particularly with respect to our law and parliamentary institution.
I think it is very dangerous to restrict freedom of speech, no matter how violent speech is, because there is a tremendous difference between violence spoken and violence acted. Sometimes I think violence spoken is a safety valve. Until recently in England freedom reached unprecedented heights at Hyde Park. I have stood in Hyde Park on a Sunday afternoon and listened to the speakers. Perhaps they were disturbed, perhaps not. Some very notable people spoke in Hyde Park, including Bernard Shaw. I heard someone say that the Queen should be eliminated from British politics. It was strange to hear this 25 years ago in Hyde Park. The English bobby walked up and down with his club. Although the fellow who was speaking was heckled, he was quite free to speak his mind. After a while he folded up the little stool on which he was standing, put it in his Cadillac or Rolls Royce and drove off.
Is there any place in the world where freedom is practised more than it is in Canada? I think not. One of the reasons is that we have an inherent desire for freedom and fair play. Whether we admit it or not, it is largely
Hate Propaganda
inherited and taught to us by those same island people, some of whom were my ancestors. My mother was born in Indian territory. She had only Indian children to play with. My grandparents and parents, aunts and uncles learned to know these first citizens of Canada well. They learned to love them and they passed that love on to me. In my family circle race tolerance is not discussed, it is practised. As far as I know, I am welcome in every Indian home in Canada and every Indian and Eskimo in Canada is welcome in my home. This is the only basis for a greater understanding of these people and their understanding of us.
My former leader, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) did not try in the Bill of Rights to codify in detail the rights of people to speak. He took it for granted that we have the right to speak. I agree. Those who speak with prejudice and hatred in their hearts are more to be pitied than a homosexual, because a homosexual does not have any control. Ignorance can be controlled. We can learn to know the people who live in our country. If we learn to know them, we will learn to love them. No statute, no matter how fierce or wise, can substitute for human understanding and human love.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I mentioned that I was a soldier. I know that in my human frailty I can be whipped up into a frenzy of patriotism, and I suppose I would fight again in defence of my home and my country. But I realize that most war is absolutely futile because it is based on hatred. As Nurse Cavell said when she was being led away to be shot for helping to free Canadian soldiers and send them back to the rich life here, "Patriotism is not enough". It was not until I reached the wrong side of 50 that I fully realized what she meant. Indeed, patriotism is not enough.
Being a soldier under arms is not enough. Being an officer of the law is not enough, whether you pound a beat or whether you sit on the Supreme Court of Canada, unless you carry into your private life, into your politics and into your relationships from Halifax to Vancouver a real sense of brotherhood based on love and understanding which can only come from meeting with people, working with them, serving with them and trying to know them better.
Sometimes the greatest heroes are not those who walk into machine-gun fire. Equal courage is shown by people of ethnic origin, many

April 7. 1970
Hate Propaganda
of whom I have had the pleasure of living with in Canada, who have endured insults from early childhood to manhood, enduring it in their home lives as well as in their public lives but showing by their tolerance that they are a good deal bigger than those who throw ignorant epithets at them. Many of these people-some of them have sat in this House- feel there is no need to codify something which warms their hearts every time they look at a flagpole and see our flag, whether it is the new one or the one they first learned to love and trust, the one that flew over our ports and over the ships which brought them here.
If I thought for one moment that passing a statute would reduce hatred in the slightest degree, I would vote for it. If I thought that any amendment to this proposed statute would reduce ill feeling among Canadians, I would vote for it. This is a question which crosses party lines: it does in my case. I am under no pressure whatever from my party to do anything but vote according to my conscience, as I intend to do, and I hope this is the feeling throughout the House. I just cannot give my support to what is second best-to trying to accomplish by laws, whether fierce or innocuous, when the alternative is to lead in a positive way along the path to friendship and better understanding.
As is often the case, we do not have a clearcut decision to make. We are sometimes offered a package deal and we are told it is not political sense to vote one way or another. I do not believe most members are attacking this problem in that manner. I do not believe this statute would ever be invoked by a government or by the law enforcement officers if they put their priorities into proper perspective. If there are people walking about who feel genocide is acceptable in the slightest degree, I claim they are sick; they need attention. This may not mean locking them up in institutions or putting the tag of mental instability upon them. It is a tag of ignorance. They, perhaps more than the victims of their evil propaganda, require our sympathy.
As far as I can see. nothing is to be gained by turning from hatred on the one side or spending time and trouble in arming ourselves to fight with imprisonment, fines and more hatred the very thing we should be attempting to attack with a great more understanding and wisdom than perhaps we now possess. So often it appears easier for us to grasp a weapon, whether it is the reeking tube or the iron shard, to settle our differ-

ences than to try once more by friendship and understanding to get through to the people we despise the most.
I find it hard not to hate people who preach race hatred, but as soon as I fall into that trap I am in a bottomless bog with them, and when one fights them on that ground there is no way of doing it except by getting down in the bog and wallowing there. Throughout recorded history men have resorted to violence. And how far have they got? With all our modern technologies, with all our provision for free education, with all our permissiveness to young people, allowing them to expand their personalities and to alleviate their pain with various drugs, with all our concern for family planning and better nutrition, with all the wonderful advances we have made in transportation, how much closer are we to the brotherhood of man?
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
These are matters we should think about. Instead of new or antiquated laws to bolster up what is perhaps an out-of-date Criminal Code, one we seem to think is inadequate in most of its aspects, we attempt in this session of Parliament-one that is becoming very liberal in many ways-by imposing penalties on people who are ignorant, undeveloped, who do not appear to have the ability to grow up mentally, politically, and certainly spiritually, to find the answer to this age old problem of brotherhood. I do not think this approach will work. I think I have the right to speak because I am nearing the age of 60, and if I have learned anything in my 60 years it is that violence begets violence, that hatred begets hatred, that misunderstanding begets misunderstanding.
In all the years I tried to enforce the Criminal Code of Canada and to make the world free for democracy, I saw more good accomplished by a few kind acts, by putting out the hand of friendship, by using a little human understanding, than all that the brass buttons, red coats and the arsenals of democracy in the western world could produce by force or law.
Although I do not think our present approach will work, I think the other approach will. In this regard I appeal to the press. This is one area in which the press can well take a hand and help us. If a man is so bigoted as to advocate racial discrimination, superiority of colour and skill, superiority of ethnic origin, he should be ridiculed. There is nothing particularly cruel about that sort of ridicule.
April 7, 1970

I feel sorry for such a person if he is mentally undeveloped. I feel sorry for him if he has come from a home where there was no love. I feel sorry for him if his free education in a modern school has left him high and dry so that he is an unfeeling wretch. This person enters a free society-as free as we can make it-where there is opportunity for people of all ethnic origins, certainly as far as I know. I beg the media to ridicule such a person, and if he is mentally sick I hope we can send him to the appropriate doctor.
It would be wasting the time of the courts to bring persons of mature years before the bench in order to tell them their basic responsibilities as Canadian citizens; to tell them they do not appreciate what freedom really is, that they do not understand what it is to be able to travel in a country such as ours where people do not have to lock their doors at night. This is a country where, by and large, both the person and his property are sacred.
I appeal to the press, to the television medium and writers of plays and singers of songs to ridicule these people. Seven years of fighting them with guns has not seemed to do much good. I do not think the violence we have seen during the last 50 years has moved us one inch closer to the brotherhood of man. But men like Martin Luther King have done so. If we needed any further proof that the black man is our equal or our superior, where is there a man today who can replace Martin Luther King?

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could not have ended on a better note.

Mr. Speaker, my reason for participating in this debate is that four or five years ago I was concerned in proceedings conducted under the Post Office Act leading to the issuance of a prohibitory order against the circulation in this country of what was called scurrilous literature. These proceedings are referred to in the report of the Special Committee on Hate Propaganda, and more particularly at pages 47 to 50.
Hate Propaganda
When I first approached this subject I was like many of the writers of editorials in our newspapers who have been giving us advice in the past few days. I thought that any effort by the state or by the criminal process to control what might be considered to be the expression of political opinion was likely to be harmful to us all. But as a result of my involvement in these proceedings I was for a considerable period of time exposed to the hideous subculture of hate-hate as expressed in the outpourings of the authors of the publications that we had to consider and which were made public by an organization called the National States Rights Party. I was also exposed to the full force and vigour of the hideous hatred of the representatives of this party in Canada.
The result of this experience was to convince me that people who offered documents of this kind and who spoke opinions of this kind were not entitled to the protection of the ordinary democratic rules and principles; that these people, at least in my opinion, were enemies of a free society and that it was in the public interest that something should be done to control what they were trying to say or trying to publish.
We are now faced with this new and important proposal, and no one can say that it has not been well considered. It has been considered by an important committee which held public hearings, which published a report that has been before the public for three or four years. As we all know, a bill in a form somewhat similar to the one presented to us now was considered for two or three years by Their Honours in the other place. This bill-I speak now as a member of the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee- received very careful consideration in committee and, I would make so bold as to say, has been improved as a result of the discussion held and suggestions made there.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
We are faced with a proposal in an amendment moved by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) which would have the effect of deleting from this bill its two most important provisions, those which prohibit public incitement of hatred and permit the authorities to impound, seize and otherwise prevent the circulation of written material expressing hatred. I find it very difficult to believe that people who have read this bill carefully could think it could be directed at the innocent and the honest expression of

April 7, 1970
Hate Propaganda
free political opinion. The opening words of proposed Section 267B are as follows:
Every one who, by communicating statements in any public place, incites hatred against any identifiable group, where such incitement is likely to lead to a breach of the peace, is guilty of-
It goes on to say that certain defences are provided, such as the defence of truth, the defence of expressing arguments which are in the public interest, and the defence of expressing arguments which are made in good faith. I have risen to speak in this debate simply because, as I said earlier, I have had first-hand exposure to written hatred, to personal hatred and to the application of the judicial or semi-judicial process to it.
I am not troubled at all by the wording of this bill. I do not have the same difficulty that has been expressed by other members about the various defences because, for what my experience is worth, the wording is not very difficult and it certainly would not be very difficult for the judiciary of this country to deal effectively with people charged under these provisions and to consider such defences as truth, good faith and the expression of argument made in the public interest. These are things experienced judges can easily ascertain, assess and apply in the circumstances presented to them. In the proceedings with which I was connected all these defences were raised, yet it was not difficult for the expert tribunal which considered the matter to put them in proper perspective and find that they did not apply.
I therefore welcome the opportunity to support the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) and others who have said that this kind of legislation can be enacted in good heart by this House. It is important for Parliament to set a standard, and the prohibition of hatred expressed in an odious and terrible way is as important to this Parliament as our Criminal Code provisions against blasphemy, criminal libel and seditious utterances. For these reasons I urge the House to reject the amendment of the hon. member for Calgary North and to support the bill.
Mr. Speaker, because it is almost ten o'clock and any remarks I make at this time will barely introduce my speech, I suggest we call it ten o'clock.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-INQUIRY AS TO TABLING OF WHITE PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the highlights in the Speech from the Throne at the opening of this session-and it will be found at page 2 of Hansard for Thursday, October 23, 1969-was the declaration that a white paper on social security would be presented to Parliament during the course of this session.
I may remind the House that in the previous session there had come to our knowledge the fact that a document known as the Willard report was being prepared. I expressed the hope that that report might be tabled during that session of Parliament, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) held out the hope that that might be done. However, it now appears that the government has no intention of making public the Willard report. Rather, the government has fallen back to its promise to make public its own white paper on social security which presumably will be based on its study of the Willard report.
As I have already said, the commitment to table the white paper in the course of this session was one of the promises in the Speech from the Throne, and hon. members will not be surprised if I say I have been asking for it just about every month since this session began. The first occasion was on Monday, October 27, 1969, as recorded at page 95 of Hansard when I asked again about the Willard report only to be told that we could not
April 7, 1970

count on seeing it, but I was reminded that there would be a white paper on social security and I quote these words from the Minister of National Health and Welfare:
-which will be brought before Parliament in the course of the next few months.
As I say, that was on October 27, 1969. I will not take the time of the House or take my own time to read all the questions I have asked during the last several months about this, but if I did they would tell the story of a receding hope. A long time ago we were to get the Willard report; then it was changed to the white paper; we were going to get a white paper soon; we were going to get it during the course of the session; we were going to get it within a few months, for after all it was a highlight of the Throne Speech. As the months have gone on, the hope that we would see that white paper in time for anything to be done on the basis of it during the course of this session seems to be disappearing.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
The last occasion I questioned about this was on Wednesday, March 25,	1970, as
recorded in Hansard at page 5466. On that day I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare if we could look forward to the tabling of the white paper on social security when we came back after the Easter recess. The minister's answer was in these words:
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe the white paper will be ready by the time the hon. member indicated.
My colleague the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) came in with a supplementary question, asking on what date we would get the white paper. The minister's reply to her was as follows:
The only assurance I can give, Mr. Speaker, is that it will be ready before the end of this session.
Then I put this supplementary question:
Will it be in time for any action to be taken on it during this session?
To that the minister replied:
I do not believe so, Mr. Speaker.
Sir, I contend that is a very sad reflection of the government's position with regard to the old age pensioners and other people in this country who look for progress in the field of social security. This document, the white paper, was held out to us in the Speech from the Throne last October as one of the high-22218- 10i
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion lights in this session. We have asked for it repeatedly and now are told we will not get it in time for anything to be done in respect of it during the course of this session. I suppose it probably will be tabled during the last week of the session so that then it will receive newspaper coverage and all that kind of thing, in the hope that the people of Canada will think something may be done about it at the next session.
In view of the length of time it takes to get a white paper, I expect we will go through another session trying to get the government to bring in its legislation. This is really reprehensible, particularly in view of a certain piece of legislation that was put through Parliament just before Easter having to do with our own pensions. We did not have to wait for a white paper on social security, but the old age pensioners are being told they must wait for that document.
This applies not only to them but also to the veterans receiving war veterans allowance. They are being told that their case cannot be considered in conjunction with the study of the Woods report or the white paper on veterans legislation. They must wait until we have the white paper on social security. In other words, there are many hundreds of thousands of people involved, when we consider those on the old age pension. Remember that three-quarters of a million of them are in such straitened circumstances that they are able to qualify for the guaranteed income supplement. When we add to that number those on the war veterans allowance and the many others who are on the borderline in need of increases in their pensions, it is a conservative estimate that at least one million people in Canada are having to wait for the tabling of the white paper for an improvement in their economic position.
Yet the government cannot bring down the white paper. I am being charitable when I say the government cannot bring it down. I contend that the government refuses to bring it down. I believe the government has made a deliberate decision, that if it is to do anything at all in this field, it will stall until as close as possible to the next election. We have had far too much of this over the course of the years. It is all right to talk about having to fight inflation and having to enlist the old age pensioners and the war veterans in the battle against inflation, but we did not join it ourselves by what we did just before Easter. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say this is a policy the government should not pursue, the policy of delaying the tabling of the white paper.

I know that the white paper when it comes down will not by itself do anything. I know that after that there has to be legislation. I am not one who expects to be greatly delighted by the white paper, for I believe it will probably say some things that are grossly inadequate. But if the government has decided that the tabling of its white paper is the next step before there can be legislation in this field, then for heaven's sake bring it down so that we can get on with pension legislation and do something positive to meet the needs of more than one million people who are waiting desperately for action in this field.
