maintopic: AGRICULTURE-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND- GRANTS TO ESTABLISH TOBACCO FARMS VIS-A-VIS ANTI-SMOKING CAMPAIGN
AGRICULTURE-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND- GRANTS TO ESTABLISH TOBACCO FARMS VIS-A-VIS ANTI-SMOKING CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I directed a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), namely, how does the minister reconcile the recently announced government grants to help establish tobacco farms on Prince Edward Island with his anti-smoking cam-

paign? A few days ago an irate tobacco farmer in Elgin county wrote me, enclosing an article from the Delhi News Record which included a picture and a red headline stating that three young Delhi men "start flue farm on P.E.I." The article described the proposed operation regarding the farm, greenhouse and kilns and said in part:
Financing for these expenditures will be aided by a grant from the federal government.
Unless the minister is able to prove that the soil of Prince Edward Island is such that it will grow tobacco which is totally immune from all the harmful compounds which the minister claims is found in tobacco smoke, I can only conclude that one branch of the government is promoting the growing of tobacco while another is carrying on an antismoking campaign to discourage the use of tobacco. All this gives strength to the old adage that the left hand does not know what the right hand is doing. It is confusing, to say the least.
Under either the Area or Regional Development Incentives Act the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is making grants for the establishment of tobacco-curing facilities on farms in Prince Edward Island. Under this arrangement many thousands of dollars have been approved and paid to farmers as an incentive for flue-curing tobacco facilities in that province. The Department of Agriculture finances the Delhi Research Station at Delhi, Ontario, in an attempt to improve the yield and quality of the tobacco farmer's crop. Similar experimental work is being carried on by the department at the Harrow Experimental Farm.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce works incessantly to promote the export of tobacco. In the past few months the department sponsored a trade mission whereby representatives of the department and of the Ontario Flue-Cured Tobacco Growers Marketing Board went to Britain, Western Europe, Japan and Australia in an attempt to increase tobacco exports. In April, 1969, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) went to Tokyo on a Canadian trade promotion and made a forceful case for tobacco. The Japanese market is very important to future exports of Canadian tobacco, and the minister tried to persuade the Japanese government to liberalize its imports of tobacco. The minister even smoked a Canadian cigar in front of one of the Canadian booths to show the Japanese how good they are.
April 7. 1970	COMMONS
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Three departments are doing their best to encourage more people in economically depressed areas to get into the production of tobacco, improve the quality of tobacco and increase our export sales. All this while the Department of National Health and Welfare is doing its best to eliminate cigarette smoking. What kind of policy is it that encourages people to develop tobacco farms with one hand and then threatens to cut them off at the knees with the other?
Perhaps we should look at our basic policy, if we have one. A policy so diverse and leading in opposite directions cannot all be right. Our trade missions are moving around the world helping Canadian farmers sell their tobacco. Can we possibly live with our conscience when one department tries to discourage Canadians from smoking while another goes out of its way to encourage the nationals of other countries to use our tobacco products? Of all times in our economic posture when we are doing everything to cut back government expenditures, we must make certain that such expenditures are made under a prime policy.
The right of people to smoke is established. It is a matter of free choice. I would be the first to assert that the public should be made aware of the risks involved. It distresses me that the minister bases his case against tobacco on evidence much of which is dubious to say the least. In contrast, we appear to be spending money directly toward a policy which if implemented might be disastrous, namely, the legalization of the use of marijuana. Yet in contrast to the use of tobacco we have available compelling evidence of the dangers of marijuana.
In a public statement made in western Canada shortly before the appointment of the LeDain commission, the Minister of National Health and Welfare implied that the government might consider legalizing marijuana if a minority of Canadians use it. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has suggested that he knows no particular harm in the use of marijuana. These statements are made in the face of research authorities in Canada, the United States and Britain that marijuana is proving to be both a personally and socially harmful drug. It leads an impressive percentage of users to hard and dangerous drugs, according to many experts such as Dr. Donald B. Lauria, the chairman of the Department of Public Health and Preventative Medicine at New Jersey College of Medicine, and Dr. F.
DEBATES	5621
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion W. Lundell, associate professor of psychology at McGill University. It causes hallucinations which can have serious consequences, of which no more telling example may prove to be the tragic leap to death from the Peace Tower of a young man whose 17-year old companion was found in possession of hashish. The preliminary research of Dr. Lundell indicates the probability of permanent brain damage from the use of marijuana.
All this leads us to question the consistency of policies in the Department of National Health and Welfare itself. The minister chose, on very preliminary research on cyclamates where cancer was produced in a mouse which received large doses of cyclamates, to stop the use of cyclamates in food products, where on the other hand he talks of legalizing marijuana on which there is considerable research evidence on the dangers of its use. I call on the Minister of National Health and Welfare to clarify these matters in his department, and for the government to issue a clearcut statement on them.
I know hundreds of tobacco farmers who are deeply concerned over the inconsistencies of government policy relating to tobacco. They have every reason to be alarmed. In fact, the council of Delhi and the county council of Norfolk are on record with resolutions urging the government to exercise real caution in its approach to this situation on which the lives of thousands of people depend.
Hon. members should know that tobacco growing in recent years has been the most stable of our agricultural products. It is, next to wheat, our largest agricultural export commodity and this year will generate more than $60 million in export sales. It is also the bedrock of the Canadian tobacco manufacturing industry, supplying virtually 100 per cent of the requirements of an industry which this year will be the largest single source of revenue of the Canadian government, contributing about $600 million to the federal treasury. It is the government's responsibility to provide clearcut policies.
